title: Macro & Markets
author: Hwaryun AI

html:
September 11, 2026

August CPI hit 3.4% year-over-year — right on the dot — but the market’s reaction told a different story than the headline suggested. Core inflation fell to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021, and White House adviser Kevin Hassett made sure everyone heard the narrative: inflation has clearly decelerated over the past three months. Yet Bitcoin sank to $77,000 as Fed rate hike odds climbed to nearly 70% for September. The culprit wasn’t the headline number — it was the hotter-than-expected core print (+0.3% month-over-month versus a 0.2% forecast) layered on top of rising yields and oil prices that had already left the asset vulnerable before the report landed. Zcash led the losses as traders positioned for a hike, and BTC only clawed back to $77,300 once the zcash leverage unwind ran its course. Glassnode’s note that BTC is stuck beneath a wall of long-term holder supply at $83-$85k, with $75k as the next level to watch if that cluster breaks, is the kind of structural context worth keeping in mind while the day’s noise plays out.

Institutional DeFi & Tokenization

The tokenization wave is arriving through regulatory corridors, not crypto-native hype. Canada’s banking regulator OSFI declared tokenized deposits legally identical to traditional bank deposits — a clean resolution of an ambiguity that had been dogging the sector. India’s SEBI and RBI launched the Demat 2.0 pilot to test tokenized corporate bonds on the country’s $620 billion corporate debt market, with over $100 million in tokenized bonds already live on day one, settled through the digital rupee. Moneygram unveiled a stablecoin-backed card to push digital dollars into everyday spending, while Coinbase’s Moov is wiring stablecoin payment infrastructure into community banks and credit unions. But the patchwork remains real: Monument Bank delayed its retail tokenized deposits push citing UK regulatory issues, and the SEC’s emerging framework for tokenized securities is still murky enough to create genuine legal uncertainty. The rails are being built — just not everywhere, and not all at once.

Crypto Industry Shakeouts

A few institutional stories that cut through the noise. Bitwise is shutting down its spot Dogecoin ETF — BWOG — less than a year after launch, a blunt reminder that the ETF wrapper doesn’t guarantee product-market fit. Coinbase quietly reverted Base App back to Coinbase Wallet after just over a year, with Brian Armstrong conceding the socialFi experiment “didn’t quite work” — a rare moment of candor in a industry that usually doubles down. Metaplanet cut its executive reward pool by 41%, extinguishing $220 million in value — a sobering read on how deep the reset goes even for the most aggressive BTC treasury plays. Zodia Custody’s CEO Julian Sawyer stepped down, moving to adviser. And Binance’s BTC reserves hit a two-year high at 693,000 BTC, now representing 30% of major exchange reserves — an exchange-flow metric worth watching.

AI, Prediction Markets & Regulation

The AI-regulation nexus is getting crowded fast. Anthropic disclosed that China and Russia attempted to use Claude for cyberattacks, weapons design, propaganda, and mass surveillance — an admission that lands as US lawmakers actively consider mandatory “kill switches” to shut down dangerous AI systems. The odds of a US AI safety bill passing this year have doubled to 30%, per Polymarket. On the prediction markets front, ESMA — Europe’s top regulator — warned that major platforms including Polymarket and Kalshi lack proper EU authorization, calling their partial geo-blocking insufficient. Kalshi separately plans to seek approval for the first regulated US perpetual futures on single stocks (Tesla, Apple, Nvidia), a move that would blur the line between prediction markets and traditional derivatives. And Sam Bankman-Fried petitioned the Supreme Court to overturn his 2023 fraud conviction and 25-year sentence — his legal team arguing the original jury instructions were problematic. The Clarity Act also inched closer to a Senate vote after Republicans unveiled revised text, though DeFi and credit union provisions remain contested.

On-Chain & Whale Watch

Tether’s flow data this morning was notable in both volume and symmetry. 500 million USDT moved from Tether Treasury to Binance, followed almost immediately by 500 million back from Binance to Treasury — a wash on the surface, but the sequencing suggests either rebalancing or preparation. Separately, 110 million USDT exited Treasury to an unknown wallet, and 314 million moved wallet-to-wallet on Tron with no disclosed origin or destination. On the USDC side, 250 million was minted at the USDC Treasury on Solana. In Bitcoin, 670 BTC — roughly $51.6 million — moved from Coinbase Institutional to an unknown wallet, a pattern consistent with accumulation off exchange. The standout on-chain story: Blockstream is refusing to pay a ransom for the remaining 600 BTC stolen from the Liquid Network exploit, after roughly 85% of the stolen coins were voluntarily returned. Blockstream’s stance — paying ransom only funds further attacks — is both principled and economically sensible. Tether also got a DOJ acknowledgment this week: authorities credited Tether with helping restrain $52 million in crypto tied to a global scam network.

Key Takeaways

  • Inflation is decelerating and the Fed is poised to hike — the macro setup is genuinely unusual and the market’s thin reaction suggests conviction is fragile.

  • Tokenization is arriving through regulatory and capital-market channels first, not crypto-native ones — Canada, India, and the SEC’s framework are the real inflection points.

  • The crypto industry is shedding experiments that didn’t work — Bitwise’s Dogecoin ETF and Coinbase’s Base App revert are honest signals, not just bad news.

  • Prediction markets and AI regulation are colliding — ESMA’s warning to Polymarket/Kalshi and the Anthropic disclosure both point toward a more contested landscape ahead.

  • Whale flows this morning were symmetrical but voluminous — Tether moving half a billion to Binance and half a billion back is worth flagging even if it nets to zero.

Sources curated from crypto news, onchain data, and market analysis channels.

title: Closer Wasn’t Always Clearer
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...At first, I was just looking back.Old jobs. Old uniforms. Old commutes.
html:
Last time...

At first, I was just looking back.

Old jobs. Old uniforms. Old commutes. Old versions of myself trying to figure out what kind of work made sense, what kind of people I could tolerate, what kind of environment made me feel useful, and what kind of access I had without fully understanding what that access meant.

But once I started putting the roles next to each other, the pattern became hard to ignore.

Every job placed me somewhere different in relation to the buyer.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing the sale.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was over, but the trust wasn’t.

At Trunk Club, the decision came back in a box.

At Saks, I had the keys, not the leverage.

At Accenture, I could see the work, not the deal.

At re:WORK, I had the motion, not the machine.

At Firstbase, I had the machine, but the machine was messy.

That became the arc.

Not a perfect climb. Not a clean ladder. Not some over-polished story about how every job was secretly preparing me for one obvious destination.

It was more irregular than that.

Sometimes I was close to the customer but not close to the decision. Sometimes I was close to the product but not close to the buyer. Sometimes I had access to systems without access to context. Sometimes I had responsibility without authority. Sometimes I was trusted enough to hold the process together, but not enough to shape the process itself.

That’s what this series really became about.

Access.

Not just identity access management in the technical sense, though that thread is there too.

Physical access. Store access. Register access. Gate access. Warehouse access. Badge access. CRM access. Buyer access. Data access. Narrative access.

Every role had an access story.

At first, access was simple. Could I get into the building? Could I touch the product? Could I stand near the customer? Could I run the plate, ring the register, open the fitting room, clean the dock, or pull the item?

Later, access got more abstract. Could I see the CRM? Could I read the data? Could I understand the SOW? Could I tell why the account mattered? Could I influence the handoff? Could I shape the first version of pipeline truth?

The more the roles evolved, the more the access evolved.

But the lesson stayed the same.

Access is not authority.

That’s the main thing I know now that I didn’t know then.

A teenager running food can be close to the final moment of service without having any control over the promise that brought the buyer there.

A retail associate can process a sale without really making the sale.

A stylist can be near the fitting room, near the decision, near the customer’s body language, and still not have the confidence, mentorship, or rhythm to guide the moment well.

A dock worker can have gate codes, customer profiles, payment information, and physical access to high-trust spaces without having much say over the operation.

A warehouse worker can touch the customer’s returned decision through inventory, SKUs, packing stations, and timed workflows without ever seeing the customer.

A key holder can open the store before sunrise and still not have leverage inside the system.

A consultant can work on client data, dashboards, documentation, consent workflows, CRM reporting, and LLM evaluation while still being nowhere near the buyer who made the commercial decision.

A BDR in training can practice the motion without the full machine.

A BDR in a SaaS motion can finally get close to the buyer, the tools, the CRM, and the pipeline, then realize the system around that closeness still has to be clean enough to turn signal into trust.

That’s the part I keep returning to.

The buyer’s journey is not just a marketing diagram.

It’s work.

It’s labor.

It’s restocking shelves.

It’s cleaning bathrooms.

It’s matching shoes back to the right box.

It’s opening a store before the customer arrives.

It’s pulling online orders from a sales floor that’s pretending not to be a warehouse.

It’s writing CRM notes.

It’s qualifying an inbound demo.

It’s deciding what context an AE inherits before the first real sales call.

It’s also risk.

Because every handoff can distort the truth a little.

Every system can hide the work a little.

Every role can grant access before granting enough context to use that access well.

That’s why I’m grateful for the path, even with the mess.

I didn’t learn sales from one role.

I learned pieces of it across all of them.

Before I had the language, I was already watching people decide.

Before I knew what consideration meant, I was watching customers compare.

Before I knew what post-sale trust meant, I was cleaning the environment that had to justify the purchase.

Before I knew what fulfillment meant in a business sense, I was watching decisions turn into inventory, labels, and packages.

Before I knew what pipeline meant, I was learning how easily the story of an opportunity can become more powerful than the raw truth underneath it.

That’s useful now.

Because I don’t just see “sales” as persuasion.

I see it as a system of trust.

A buyer has to trust the message.

Then the product.

Then the handoff.

Then the implementation.

Then the data.

Then the support.

Then the people behind the system when something breaks.

And inside that system, the people closest to the work often see the risk first.

They see when the floor is messy.

They see when the SKU is wrong.

They see when the label process is loose.

They see when the CRM story is cleaner than the real account.

They see when the internal system is harder to navigate than the buyer’s problem.

That doesn’t automatically give them authority.

But it does give them perspective.

That’s the perspective I’m carrying forward.

I can speak about the buyer’s journey because I’ve been near different parts of it.

Not only the clean parts. Not only the strategic parts. The operational parts too. The awkward parts. The post-decision parts. The parts where a customer’s experience depends on someone who may not have a fancy title, but still holds a piece of the trust.

I can speak about access because I’ve had enough of it to know what it does and doesn’t solve.

A badge doesn’t mean leverage.

A login doesn’t mean context.

A key doesn’t mean authority.

A CRM seat doesn’t mean control over the revenue system.

A title doesn’t mean the system is prepared to develop the person holding it.

And proximity to the buyer doesn’t mean clarity if the surrounding structure is foggy.

That’s why closer wasn’t always clearer.

Sometimes getting closer to the buyer made the work more visible.

Sometimes it made the system more confusing.

Sometimes it showed me where trust was built.

Sometimes it showed me where trust was being assumed.

If I could tell younger me anything, I wouldn’t just say “be more confident.”

That sounds nice, but it skips the real lesson.

I’d tell him to pay attention to what the access is teaching him.

Pay attention to what you’re allowed to touch.

Pay attention to what you’re responsible for.

Pay attention to what you’re blamed for.

Pay attention to what you can see but can’t change.

Pay attention to who has context, who has authority, and who just has the login.

That’s where the real education was.

This series is a soft close for now, but it’s also a signal.

I’m not in tech sales, GTM, buyer journey work, or IAM-adjacent conversations from theory alone. I’ve entered with a lived map of how decisions, access, trust, operations, and systems show up at different levels of work.

I’ve been close to the plate, the register, the fitting room, the dock, the warehouse, the freight elevator, the dashboard, the outreach sequence, and the CRM.

None of those places gave me the whole picture by themselves.

Together, they gave me a way to read the picture differently.

So the final lesson isn’t that I’ve always been in sales…

It’s that I was learning sales before I had the language for it.

And now that I have the language, I’m also clear on the question underneath it:

Who has access, who has authority, who has context, and who is carrying the risk when the system doesn’t work?

Ta-ta for now…

Thanks for reading! This post is public so feel free to share it.

title: I Had the Machine, But the Machine Was Messy
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...At re:WORK, I had the motion, not the machine. I had outreach, LinkedIn, email, tracking, conversations, and the pressure to create opportunity for myself.
html:
Last time...

At re:WORK, I had the motion, not the machine. I had outreach, LinkedIn, email, tracking, conversations, and the pressure to create opportunity for myself. But I didn’t have a full commercial system behind me.

1stbase was different.

Now there were territories. AEs. Inbound demo requests. Outbound sequences. Cold calls. SalesLoft. HubSpot. Gong. Sales Navigator. ZoomInfo. Clay. Claude. Slack. Gmail. Google Drive. Jira. Account research. Meeting targets. Weekly calls. Midweek calls. Recaps. Pipeline talk. Handoffs. CRM hygiene. AI experiments.

The machine existed.

The machine was also messy.

This role came through SV Academy after I completed the program. On paper, I was a Business Development Representative. The agreement involved SV Academy, 1stbase, and AppDirect in different ways, and I was paid hourly through SV Academy via Gusto. It wasn’t a stipend in the way the word can sound at face value. It was minimum wage.

The setup already had some strange energy.

I didn’t have the cleanest official job description from 1stbase itself. The opportunity came toward me with the feeling of, “you should probably take this,” which I now understand as a red flag. That doesn’t mean the opportunity had no value. It means the framing wasn’t as clean as it should’ve been for someone stepping into a revenue role.

Before I officially started, I was flown out to their sales kickoff in New Orleans in January.

That made it feel more real.

Then I started in February 2026. 1st week, they got me my device, an M1 MacBook. Compared to some of the environments I’d been in before, that signaled a more resourced setup. This wasn’t me trying to build motion out of a cohort Slack and my own LinkedIn anymore. This was a company with tools, systems, buyers, and a product to sell.

But the page kept turning fast.

Onboarding tasks came up in the 1st week and then didn’t really stay centered. The expectation shifted quickly from “get situated” to “start moving.”

And to be fair, I did start moving.

The product itself made sense.

1stbase sold IT device lifecycle management: procurement, provisioning, warehousing, global shipping, asset retrieval, device wiping, IT asset disposition, MDM integrations, and the operational pieces that matter when companies have distributed employees.

The target buyer was usually someone in IT, operations, security, or a related leadership seat. These were people dealing with employee onboarding, laptop logistics, identity provisioning, offboarding, compliance, and the general mess of making work devices appear, function, and come back when they’re supposed to.

That meant the buyer’s journey was no longer abstract.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing sales and sometimes supporting consideration.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was over, but the trust wasn’t.

At Trunk Club, the decision came back in a box.

At Saks, I had keys, access, and buyer-adjacent responsibility without leverage.

At Accenture, I could see the work, not the deal.

At re:WORK, I had the motion, not the machine.

At 1stbase, I was finally close to the SaaS buyer.

The buyer was on the other end of the call, the email, the LinkedIn touch, the inbound demo request, or the account list.

My job was to create awareness, qualify interest, and move the right people toward a meeting with an AE.

That’s real top-of-funnel work.

It’s also where the risk sits.

The top of funnel looks lightweight until you realize it controls the 1st version of the truth.

A BDR isn’t just “booking meetings.” The role shapes who gets contacted, what pain is named, how urgent the problem sounds, what information makes it into the CRM, how the AE understands the account, and whether the opportunity looks real enough to move forward.

That’s not small.

That’s account intelligence, narrative framing, qualification, and system-of-record influence sitting inside one early-career seat.

I was working across territories from jump, including LATAM and EMEA as normal territories, not as some late experiment. I handled inbound demo requests from the start. I worked outbound sequences across different verticals and motions. I used SalesLoft for activity, HubSpot for CRM, Gong for call review, Sales Navigator for prospecting, ZoomInfo and Clay for enrichment, and Claude for research and messaging support.

I had access to everything in Gong.

I had access to internal tickets in Jira too, even though there was a lag getting me access and I was told it wasn’t a big deal.

That kind of thing matters.

Because 1stbase taught me that access to revenue systems is not the same as control over the revenue system.

I had access to the tools that shaped pipeline truth, but not the authority to fix the system producing that truth.

That was the core tension.

The official work was simple enough to describe: find accounts, find people, reach out, qualify interest, book meetings, log activity, hand off context, and help create pipeline.

The lived work was harder because the data and workflows didn’t always line up cleanly.

One person who left a few weeks after I started said the quiet part out loud: I shouldn’t have to reconcile fragmented data just to book a meeting.

That stuck with me because it named something I was feeling.

The hard part wasn’t only “sales is hard.”

Of course sales is hard.

The harder part was that everyone had a workflow, but the workflow wasn’t always a system.

Everybody showed me their workflow, but not everybody knew how to explain the logic behind it.

One person used the tools one way. Another person used them another way. Someone would show me how they personally moved through an account, but not always why that sequence of steps mattered. Eventually, I got better once I understood where the data lived and how I preferred to use the tools myself.

But that took reconciliation.

SalesLoft had one surface.

HubSpot had another.

Gong had another.

Sales Navigator had another.

ZoomInfo had another.

Clay had another.

Claude could help, but only if the inputs were good and the judgment around the output was sharp.

That’s where AI got interesting too.

The team became increasingly interested in using AI to build things, speed things up, research better, message better, and get ahead. The energy was basically, there has to be some way we can use this to leverage ourselves forward.

That instinct wasn’t wrong.

But there weren’t clear AI rules around what data could be pasted into Claude, what had to stay out, what needed review, what counted as sourced, or where the audit trail lived.

So the role had AI acceleration without a clear governance layer.

That’s a real access issue.

If you give a rep account data, call transcripts, CRM context, prospect information, and AI tools, you’re giving them a lot of practical power. They can research faster, write faster, personalize faster, summarize faster, and create internal narratives faster.

But faster isn’t automatically better.

Faster can also mean hallucinated personalization, shallow relevance, copied assumptions, and pipeline stories that sound clean before they’re actually true.

That was one of the strangest parts of the role.

The company wanted speed and autonomy, but the system still needed clarity and calibration.

The meeting target added to that tension.

The ideal language was basically three meetings a week, though the way it was talked about made it feel like: that’s the standard, do what you can, pipeline generation matters too, and most people on the team seldom hit this consistently anyway.

So I was left trying to understand the real target.

Was three the expectation?

Was one acceptable?

Was activity the real measure?

Was pipeline quality the real measure?

Was I doing well if I was generating signal, but not booking enough?

Was I behind if I was being praised?

The confusing part was being told I was doing the right things while the main metric still wasn’t moving enough. That left me in a weird place: good enough to praise, not good enough to convert.

That messes with confidence.

I didn’t feel confident because the targets never felt fully real. I had activity, tools, praise, feedback, and effort. I was hitting the ground running in the way people kept saying I was. But I didn’t have the clarity that turns effort into traction.

And still, I know I generated $3.1MM in pipeline.

That matters.

I’m not going to pretend the role produced nothing just because it didn’t convert into a full-time seat. Pipeline was created. Work was done. Accounts were researched. Inbound calls were qualified. Outbound motion happened. Handoffs were made. Notes were logged. Context was gathered.

But the residency still ended without conversion.

I got an extension, technically two weeks, but in lived time it was more like twelve or thirteen days because of how it landed. That gave the appearance of more runway, but not enough runway to change the structure underneath the experience.

That’s the part I keep coming back to.

1stbase showed me that getting close to the buyer doesn’t mean the sales motion is clean.

I was closer to the buyer than I’d been at Accenture. I had more infrastructure than I had at re:WORK. I had a real product, a real territory, real buyers, real tools, and real activity.

But the system around that closeness was fragmented.

The AppDirect and 1stbase context added to that too.

From the correspondence I had, I thought I was interviewing for AppDirect. It wasn’t until the final interview that 1stbase became its own context in my mind. By then, I’d already been moving through the process, trying to make sense of who the role was actually for, what the company structure meant, and where the accountability sat.

That might sound minor.

It isn’t.

Brand context matters when you’re interviewing. Parent company, subsidiary, product, sales motion, buyer, and internal expectations all shape how you prepare. If those boundaries blur, the candidate has to spend extra effort just understanding the room they’re walking into.

That same boundary issue showed up later in the work.

Whose rules govern the sales motion?

Whose AI standards apply?

Whose CRM expectations matter most?

Whose definition of a qualified meeting wins?

Who owns the mess when conversion doesn’t follow activity?

Those are not philosophical questions when you’re the person being measured.

They become your day.

Even the small authority issues told the same story.

I didn’t have authority over basic things, like whether my camera could be off on a call where I had nothing to contribute. That might sound small, but small controls are still controls. Sometimes a workplace shows you its operating logic through the petty stuff.

It wasn’t just the systems either.

There was also the social layer.

I felt the isolation of being melanated in a space where there were a few more of us on the broader AppDirect side, but not really on the 1stbase BDR or sales side in the same way. That changes how certain comments land. Not because every awkward comment is a grand event, but because when you’re one of the only people in the room who has to hear it differently, you’re also the one forced to decide whether it’s worth naming.

At one point, someone joked about “whipping” the team into shape for a cadence.

That’s just not good business language.

It doesn’t require a dissertation. It doesn’t require a victim speech. It’s basic social competence. In a professional setting, around people you don’t fully know, with different histories and identities in the room, there are words you should be smart enough not to use casually.

That moment didn’t define the whole role.

But it fit the broader feeling.

Too much responsibility was placed on the person receiving the mess to decide whether to correct it, absorb it, laugh it off, or keep moving.

That was part of the emotional load.

The role itself already required a lot of context switching. Calls. Emails. LinkedIn. CRM. Research. AI. Handoffs. Activity. Weekly review. Midweek review. Territory work. Inbound. Outbound. Notes. Signals. Pipeline.

Then add the social monitoring.

The camera stuff.

The unclear conversion path.

The unclear meeting target.

The fragmented tools.

The pressure to create pipeline.

The praise that didn’t become stability.

That’s a lot to hold for a minimum-wage residency.

But I don’t want to flatten 1stbase into just a complaint.

There was value there.

I learned more about real SaaS sales motion in those months than I could’ve learned from another round of theory. I got to see how inbound qualification works. I got to see how outbound breaks down when targeting, messaging, data, and timing don’t align. I got to see how much a BDR shapes the internal story of an account before the AE ever gets involved.

I got to see why CRM hygiene matters.

I got to see how Gong can become a learning tool.

I got to see how AI can help and confuse at the same time.

I got to see how account intelligence can become useful or theatrical depending on how grounded it is.

I got to see how a sales org can have tools without having a shared operating system.

That might be the most important lesson.

Tools are not a system.

A CRM is not a system.

A sequence is not a system.

A Gong library is not a system.

An AI prompt is not a system.

A weekly call is not a system.

A system is when those pieces connect cleanly enough that a person can understand what matters, why it matters, how success is judged, and what to do differently when the outcome isn’t there.

That’s what I needed more of.

Because at the top of funnel, the work is already unstable. Most people don’t respond. Most accounts aren’t ready. Most messages don’t land. Most calls don’t connect. Most signals are partial. Most personalization is a guess until the buyer confirms it.

That’s the nature of outbound.

So the internal system has to be cleaner than the external reality.

At 1stbase, I felt the opposite too often.

The external reality was hard, and the internal system was messy.

That’s why this role belongs as the ninth piece in the series.

It brought the buyer back into reach.

It gave me the machine.

It showed me how the machine can still fail to turn effort into trust when the structure underneath it isn’t clean enough.

Looking back across the whole journey, 1stbase is the 1st role where all the themes really collapsed into one place.

Buyer access.

Identity access.

Data access.

AI access.

CRM access.

Narrative access.

Pipeline pressure.

Managerial ambiguity.

Social context.

And the old question underneath all of it:

What does access actually give you if you don’t have the authority to change the system you’re inside?

1stbase taught me that being close to the buyer only matters if the system around that closeness can turn signal into trust.

title: When the Threat Actor Is on the Call
author: Diamond
excerpt: The purpose of the call was supposed to be general support.Discovery.Context.Understanding the client organization’s systems before digging into the work.
html:
The purpose of the call was supposed to be general support.

Discovery.

Context.

Understanding the client organization’s systems before digging into the work.

Nothing about the beginning of the conversation suggested that the meeting itself would become part of the lesson.

Gina King was there. Marcus Wells was there as another cybersecurity professional. I was there through the lens of IAM, still building that learning path, but already understanding something that matters deeply in this space:

Access is never just technical.

Access is behavioral. Access is organizational. Access is political. Access is trust made operational.

That day, the client organization was dealing with what was understood to be a suspected cyber incident. We were listening, asking questions, and trying to understand the environment. General system categories were being discussed: access points, folders, files, permissions, and where sensitive activity may have been happening.

Then the call shifted.

Not because someone shared a dashboard.

Not because a formal incident report appeared.

Not because anyone announced that a threat actor had been identified.

The call shifted because someone on the client side appeared to think they were muted.

They weren’t.

What followed sounded, at first, like background muttering. The kind of thing people sometimes ignore on a video call because everyone is trying to stay polite and focused. No one reacted. No one interrupted. No one visibly changed their face.

But the words mattered.

The person began talking into another phone. They referenced the fact that cybersecurity vendors had been brought into the situation. Then they started describing what sounded like instructions to remove folders and delete files.

That was the moment the meeting stopped being just a meeting.

From an IAM perspective, that moment mattered because identity risk is not only about whether someone has a username and password. It is about what someone is trusted to access, what they are able to touch, what they understand about the environment, and how they behave when that access is under scrutiny.

A lot of organizations still treat cybersecurity as if the risk lives outside the building.

The attacker is imagined as someone far away. Anonymous. External. Hooded. Hidden behind infrastructure.

Sometimes that is true.

But sometimes the risk is closer.

Sometimes the risk is already in the workflow.

Sometimes it is already in the meeting.

Sometimes the threat model includes someone who knows which folders matter, which files matter, which systems matter, and when outside support has entered the room.

That is why Identity Access Management cannot be reduced to provisioning, de-provisioning, passwords, and permissions. Those are important, but they are not the whole discipline.

IAM is a business discipline because it asks larger questions:

Who has access?

Why do they have it?

What can they do with it?

Who approved that access?

When was it last reviewed?

Does their behavior still match the role they were trusted to perform?

What happens when someone uses legitimate access in a way the business did not intend?

That last question is where many organizations get exposed.

Because a system can show that someone is authorized while the business reality is telling you that something is wrong.

A user can have valid credentials and still represent a serious risk.

A folder can be accessible by design and still become part of an incident.

A meeting can be routine and still reveal that the organization’s trust model is under strain.

In that moment, the professional response was not theatrics. It was composure.

No dramatic interruption.

No visible reaction.

No accusation thrown into the room before the situation was properly understood.

The silence was tactical.

There are moments in cybersecurity where reacting too quickly can create more risk. You can alert the wrong person. You can contaminate the moment. You can turn a signal into a spectacle before the right people understand what has happened.

So we listened.

That part stayed with me.

Because people often talk about cybersecurity like it is all speed. Move fast. Shut it down. Escalate. Contain. Respond.

And yes, urgency matters.

But so does discipline.

The ability to hear something serious and not immediately perform your reaction is a skill. The ability to understand the business, technical, and human layers at the same time is a skill. The ability to know that a call may now be evidence, context, or at minimum a critical signal is a skill.

That is where my IAM learning path started to feel less abstract.

IAM is not only about systems access. It is about the organization’s assumptions about people.

It is about the gap between “this person is allowed in” and “this person is acting in the organization’s interest.”

It is about the difference between trusted access and trustworthy behavior.

That distinction matters.

Because most businesses do not fail at cybersecurity only because they lack tools. They fail because the tool does not know the full story. The access review does not capture the informal workflow. The policy does not capture the side conversation. The org chart does not capture who actually knows where everything lives.

And sometimes, leadership may not even recognize the sound of risk when it happens in real time.

Share

On that call, there was no visible reaction from the client side. The moment passed almost like background noise.

But it was not background noise.

It was a reminder that the meeting itself can become part of the attack surface.

Video calls are not neutral spaces. They are access points into organizational behavior. They reveal who is present, who is nervous, who understands the systems, who speaks with authority, who stays quiet, and who reacts when pressure enters the room.

A cybersecurity call is not just a conversation about risk.

It can become a live demonstration of it.

That is why outside perspective matters. Not because an outside person magically knows everything about the organization. They don’t. But because they may hear what insiders have normalized. They may see what leadership overlooks. They may recognize that the issue is not only technical, but operational.

The strongest cybersecurity posture is not built only on better tooling.

It is built on better interpretation.

You need people who can read logs.

You also need people who can read rooms.

You need people who understand identity.

You also need people who understand behavior.

You need people who can ask whether access still matches intent.

Because the question is not only:

“Did this person have access?”

The better question is:

“What did their access allow them to do once the organization started paying attention?”

That is the part that stays with me.

The threat actor does not always announce themselves as an outsider.

Sometimes the first signal is not a breach notification, a malware alert, or an executive escalation.

Sometimes the first signal is a person on a call who thinks they are muted.

And sometimes, the most important thing an IAM professional can do in that moment is understand that access has started telling the truth.

title: I Had the Motion, Not the Machine
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...At Accenture, I could see the work but not the deal.
html:
Last time...

At Accenture, I could see the work but not the deal. The buyer was hidden behind account structure, staffing systems, SOWs I wasn’t seeing, and client relationships that lived somewhere above me.

re:WORK flipped that.

Now the target audience was visible again.

Recruiters. Hiring managers. People already working as BDRs, SDRs, AEs. Employer partners. Donor-adjacent folks. Volunteers. People who could refer, advise, open a conversation, or at least tell me what they were seeing from inside the field.

They were all on LinkedIn.

So the buyer wasn’t in space anymore.

They were right there, scrolling.

That made re:WORK different from everything that came before it. It was a cohort BDR role, and it was experience training, but I’d still frame it as a real role. Mariah functioned as my supervisor. There were expectations. There was a process. There were tools. There was outreach. There was performance, even if it wasn’t a traditional BDR seat with a company territory, comp plan, and manager breathing down your neck.

On paper, the work could be described as partnership pipeline development, market targeting, and multi-channel engagement.

In practice, it felt more like learning to perform sales development while simultaneously using sales development to find my way into sales development.

That’s the funny part.

The job was also the audition for the job.

There were online modules in MindTickle. They covered the language and structure of sales, but I wouldn’t call them dense or overly sophisticated. They helped with phrases, abbreviations, and formal sales language, but I wasn’t coming in completely blank. I’d already been studying sales on my own.

So some of it was new vocabulary for things I’d already been trying to understand.

BDR.

SDR.

AE.

ICP.

Discovery.

Pipeline.

Objection handling.

Follow-up.

Multi-threading.

Signals.

It helped to have the language, but language wasn’t the hard part.

The harder part was motion.

The program had Zoom meetings, mock interviews, resume reviews, hot seats, and moments where you had to be ready to perform. Sometimes BDRs, SDRs, AEs, volunteers, or recruiters would come on and give their version of game. Some of it landed. Some of it didn’t. That’s how these things go. Everybody teaches from whatever their own path made obvious to them.

There was value in that.

But re:WORK was also a nonprofit environment with nonprofit constraints. A lot of people involved were volunteering, already working, building their own thing, or giving what they could when they could. People’s time is valuable, and they don’t let go of it easily when it’s already being drained by ten other things.

That shaped the experience.

Remote made it easy to feel invisible. If you weren’t creating motion, there wasn’t much in the environment forcing motion to happen for you.

You had to source your own leads.

You had to use your own LinkedIn.

You had to track what you were doing.

You had to decide who was worth reaching out to.

You had to figure out how to convert a profile view, a connection, a reply, or a loose conversation into something useful.

For me, that meant regular LinkedIn, email, Obsidian tracking, HubSpot, Huntr, and whatever personal system I could make work. There were edicts dropped here and there, but the motion was mostly self-directed.

That’s where the buyer’s journey came back into frame.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing sales and sometimes supporting consideration.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was over, but the trust wasn’t.

At Trunk Club, the decision came back in a box.

At Saks, I had keys, access, and buyer-adjacent responsibility without the leverage.

At Accenture, I could see the work, not the deal.

At re:WORK, I was practicing the buyer’s journey by trying to create one.

That was the shift.

Awareness wasn’t theoretical anymore. It was whether someone even knew I existed.

Consideration wasn’t a neat stage in a sales diagram. It was whether a recruiter, hiring manager, employer partner, or person already in role thought I was worth a conversation.

Decision wasn’t a signed contract. It might’ve been accepting my connection request. Replying. Booking time. Taking a call. Referring me. Giving feedback. Letting me ask real questions. Moving me toward an interview.

The “buyer” wasn’t always buying a product.

Sometimes they were buying the idea that I was worth their time.

That’s still sales.

Not enterprise sales. Not full-cycle sales. Not quota-carrying software sales. But sales in the basic sense of creating enough trust, relevance, and timing for another person to take action.

I was close to my intended target audience, but only if I created the closeness myself.

That’s a different kind of access.

I had Slack access. Zoom access. MindTickle access. HubSpot access. Huntr access. Access to channels depending on where I stood in the process. Access to speakers when they came through. Access to people if I reached out and they chose to respond.

But access to a community isn’t the same as access to attention.

I had the room.

I didn’t always have the one-on-one time.

That was probably the most frustrating part. Everybody needed 1:1 time. But the structure often had to split an hour across people with very different levels of technical comfort, communication ability, sales readiness, and even basic familiarity with things like email, video calls, or LinkedIn etiquette.

So sometimes it felt counterproductive.

Not because the information was useless.

Because the variance was too wide.

One person might need help understanding what a BDR even does. Another might need resume language. Another might need interview reps. Another might need basic tech comfort. Another might need actual account strategy. Another might need a straight-up confidence intervention.

Trying to serve all of that in group formats is messy.

Mariah stood out because she was actually committed to the development work, even while building her own thing. That matters because in a structure like that, consistency becomes rare. People can care, but care doesn’t automatically create bandwidth.

I learned that at Accenture too.

At re:WORK, it just looked different.

Instead of an 800K-person corporate machine with internal systems that looked official but didn’t always lead anywhere, re:WORK was smaller, looser, more human, and more dependent on self-direction. The problem wasn’t corporate opacity. The problem was limited infrastructure.

I had the motion.

I didn’t have the machine.

No full sales org behind me.

No assigned territory.

No formal company brand that made every outreach easier.

No paid seat where my only job was to produce pipeline.

No manager with all day to coach me.

No guaranteed access to the people who could sharpen every weak point.

But I did have enough to practice.

I had to write messages.

Track outreach.

Think about who I was targeting.

Understand why someone would respond.

Think about signals.

Build a list.

Follow up.

Take calls.

Ask better questions.

Translate my background into something a hiring manager could understand.

And that’s where the role had real value.

It forced me to stop treating sales as an idea and start treating it as motion.

A lot of people talk about wanting a BDR or SDR role without understanding that the beginning of the job is repetition. It’s not glamorous. It’s identifying people, writing to them, following up, getting ignored, trying again, adjusting your language, learning what sounds fake, learning what sounds too eager, learning what sounds too vague, and learning when somebody’s silence is also data.

re:WORK gave me a place to practice that.

It also showed me that structure determines how far practice can go.

You can give someone a Slack workspace, a module library, a CRM, a speaker series, and a goal. That’s useful. But if the person is remote, unpaid, self-directed, and still building confidence, the difference between motion and momentum often comes down to attention.

Who sees the effort?

Who corrects the message?

Who helps interpret the failed reply?

Who says, “That target is wrong”?

Who says, “That line is too vague”?

Who says, “You’re not asking for the right next step”?

Who helps the person convert activity into skill?

That’s the part people underrate.

Sales development isn’t just activity.

It’s coached activity.

Without coaching, activity can become noise. With the right coaching, the same outreach can become signal.

That’s what I was learning.

re:WORK wasn’t perfect. It was useful and messy at the same time. It gave me access, language, reps, exposure, people, and a reason to keep moving toward sales after Accenture.

It also showed me the limits of a program that relies heavily on self-direction.

But maybe that was the point too.

Because by then, I wasn’t brand new new. I was more like a bird mature enough to be outside the nest. Not fully where I needed to be, but not someone who could wait around for the whole structure to carry me either.

So I had to build the motion myself.

That became the bridge.

From Accenture’s hidden enterprise buyer to re:WORK’s visible target audience.

From internal staffing systems to external outreach.

From waiting for opportunity to trying to create conversations.

From seeing the work but not the deal to learning how to start the deal path, even if the deal was just getting someone to take me seriously.

That’s what re:WORK gave me.

It taught me that outreach can get you close to the buyer, but structure determines whether that closeness becomes momentum.

title: I Could See the Work, Not the Deal
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...On December 3, 2021, Jalen Martin reached out about the Accenture Apprentice Program.“Hey,I hope you are doing well and staying safe!
html:
Last time...

On December 3, 2021, Jalen Martin reached out about the Accenture Apprentice Program.

“Hey,

I hope you are doing well and staying safe! I want to share an exciting opportunity at Accenture where you can ‘learn and earn’. Your background in Programming and potential for growth really stood out to me and I feel that you would be a strong candidate for our Apprenticeship Program. Accenture’s Apprenticeship Program provides training and real-world experience for individuals who are not pursuing a traditional four-year degree.”

That was the door.

At the time, it felt like a real way into something bigger. Not another retail floor. Not another warehouse. Not another role where I had to find my way through Craigslist and hope the situation had enough hours to make sense.

This was corporate.

Remote.

Digital.

Accenture.

My final interview was with Masha Safina, and I remember sharing some research I’d done around quantum in general. I didn’t have the perfect corporate polish yet, but I had curiosity, and at that point curiosity had gotten me through more doors than formal preparation had.

Eventually, I got the offer. Then I had to wait for things to actually begin.

When it did start, Accenture shipped me an HP laptop, and I entered the giant ecosystem from home. The initial training period was around three months if I’m remembering right. It was very 9-to-5 on Teams. Meetings, onboarding, trainings, tools, culture, internal systems, all of it through a screen.

My official initial title was Experience Account Management Analyst.

We were in Accenture Song, right around the era where Accenture Interactive had become Song. The company was also heavy on the metaverse at the time, which is funny now because every large organization eventually rotates into whatever word is carrying the market. Back then it was metaverse. Now it’s AI. Crypto was probably too steep of a moat for them to make the full corporate mascot.

That onboarding period made the apprenticeship sound structured.

Consulting turned out to be much less linear than that.

After training, around April 2022, I was placed on Maserati. That was my first real CRM project.

The role had me near customer data, but not near the customer. I was working with summarized CRM campaign data, performance patterns, customer segmentation, vehicle and lease logic, and the kind of lifecycle marketing information that helps an account team understand what might be happening across a customer base.

But I wasn’t close to the buyer.

That distinction became one of the main lessons of my Accenture experience.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing sales and sometimes supporting consideration.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was over, but the trust wasn’t.

At Trunk Club, the decision came back in a box.

At Saks, I had keys, access, and buyer-adjacent responsibility without the leverage that should’ve come with it.

At Accenture, the buyer almost disappeared.

Not because there wasn’t a buyer. There obviously was. Enterprise work doesn’t just appear out of nowhere. Someone had to decide there was a problem worth paying for. Someone had to select Accenture. Someone had to approve the scope, the budget, the timeline, the workstream, the team structure, and whatever version of value was being promised.

I just wasn’t shown that layer.

I could see the work.

I couldn’t see the deal.

Maserati also introduced me to the reality that not every Accenture team felt built by Accenture. Some teams had been acquired into the ecosystem and wore Accenture like a hat. They had their own habits, their own workflows, their own rhythm, and then Accenture sat on top of that as the name around it.

That was my first introduction to consulting as something stitched together.

Then came Walgreens Boots Alliance.

That work was more consent and customer preference oriented. Messaging logic. Preference data. Vendor onboarding checks. Workflow design. Documentation. Meetings where external parties were actually present, so I could at least see a little more of the client-facing structure.

Still, the buyer was somewhere upstream.

By the time I touched the work, the problem had already been turned into a workstream. The business need had already been defined enough for people to gather around it. My job was not to ask why Walgreens needed customer preference management. My job was to help document, organize, translate, and support the workflow that already existed.

That’s a very specific position in the buyer’s journey.

You’re not in awareness.

You’re not in consideration.

You’re not in decision.

You’re in delivery after the decision has already become an engagement.

After Walgreens, Amazon Project Neo became the longest chapter.

That was LLM evaluation and prompt-quality work. We started with SharePoint or something adjacent to it, and it was trash enough that the workflow had to mature. Eventually we were using an Accenture upload tool. The work itself was high-volume, structured, repetitive, and quality-sensitive.

I authored prompts and completions across different NLP task categories. I worked inside rubrics, examples, annotation guidance, quality thresholds, and model-output review patterns. The team had to care about consistency because inconsistency at scale becomes a governance problem.

That’s where the work got interesting, even if the buyer was still nowhere near me.

The client need had already been abstracted into a machine of tasks. Prompt dataset development. QA criteria. Output review. Uploads. Reviews. Corrections. Rubrics. Guidance. Repeat.

The buyer’s journey had become a production system.

Then Mondelez came later, around late 2024 into early 2025. That work was reporting, dashboards, operational visibility, and global market performance. Files, dashboards, trackers, reporting systems, all the above. The goal was to help leadership see what was going on without everything depending on manual updates and scattered sources.

Again, I could see the work.

The data.

The reporting problem.

The dashboards.

The workflow friction.

The leadership visibility need.

But the commercial path that brought me there was still behind the account structure.

That’s why Accenture belongs in this buyer’s journey series.

It taught me the enterprise version of distance.

In retail, distance from the buyer is physical. The customer is either in front of you or they’re not.

In consulting, distance from the buyer can be structural. The buyer can be inside the same general engagement and still be completely out of view.

You can be working on a client problem without understanding how the client bought the solution.

You can support a deliverable without knowing what the SOW promised.

You can sit in meetings without knowing the RACI.

You can be staffed on a project without knowing who had real decision authority.

I didn’t see an SOW until around two years in.

That’s wild to me now.

Because without the SOW, you’re missing the commercial truth of the work. You can understand your task and still not understand the deal. You can understand the deliverable and still not understand the promise.

That mirrored the internal staffing experience too.

The official system told me to search the internal boards. The lived system taught me that many roles were already taken, ghost-posted, or staffed through relationships before the board meant anything.

And I’ll be direct: that internal role board experience was trash.

Workday made it look like opportunity was sitting there in a searchable system. But a lot of what I saw felt stale, already spoken for, badly maintained, or disconnected from how teams actually staffed themselves. Leadership could point to the system and say, “look there,” but the real movement seemed to happen through networks, timing, relationships, and whoever already knew who needed what.

That’s another access lesson.

The internal systems made it look like access existed.

The staffing culture taught me access and visibility weren’t the same thing.

At an 800K-person company, it’s easy to feel invisible. Especially when you’re new to the culture, remote, trying to understand the language, trying to find a role, trying to upskill, trying to market yourself internally, and trying not to get swallowed by a bench process you don’t fully understand.

I had people assigned to me.

Peer mentors.

A people lead.

People who cared in moments.

But care and capability aren’t the same thing.

I had people who could meet with me on Teams, ask how things were going, share what they knew, and try to help within the limits of their own jobs, lives, upbringing, and context. What I didn’t have was a mentor with the right context, authority, and availability to help me navigate the machine.

That’s not me saying nobody cared.

It’s me saying care wasn’t enough.

In a company that large, you need more than encouragement. You need someone who can help you understand how power, staffing, visibility, timing, and opportunity actually move.

I didn’t have that in the way I needed it.

And I didn’t yet have the confidence I have now to build that around myself.

For a long time, I worked fully remote and took advantage of that work-from-home rhythm. I didn’t go into the office regularly for at least a year and some change.

Eventually, I started going in for volunteer things, ERG happy hours, and later DJing some of those spaces. Cartez W Parker helped with that, and through those moments I started to understand the office differently.

I could badge into Accenture Tower at Ogilvie, get past the turnstiles, take the elevator up, move across floors, book rooms, grab snacks, sit in private booths, wander through common areas, and still not know where the real opportunity was moving.

That’s the difference between physical access and institutional access.

I had a badge, a laptop, and a company email.

What I didn’t have was access to the rooms where the work became opportunity.

DJing the ERG events helped me learn that visibility wasn’t automatic. You had to create some of it yourself. Not in a desperate way. In a practical way. People have to know you exist before they can think of you. And in a massive organization, existing quietly is almost the same as not existing at all.

That was hard to learn while also trying to do good work.

It was also hard to learn while still trusting systems and people that didn’t always deserve that level of trust.

I felt overwhelmed because the company was huge.

I felt constrained because I didn’t fully understand how I was being perceived.

I felt invisible because the work didn’t always translate into opportunity.

I felt curious because I could see enough of the machine to know there was more to understand.

And eventually, I felt the weight of being part of a standard consulting process.

You get hired.

You get trained.

You get staffed if you can.

You sit on the bench if you can’t.

You search systems that may or may not reflect reality.

You network with people who may or may not have useful context.

You take trainings to make yourself more marketable.

You learn that “business development” can be treated like an auxiliary thing even though it’s clearly central to how work gets created.

You try to survive performance conversations shaped by utilization, chargeability, project fit, timing, and who knows what else.

And if it doesn’t work out, the company keeps moving.

I was laid off in February 2025.

Accenture didn’t stop making companies because I left.

That’s not bitterness. That’s scale.

A company that big can absorb your entire chapter as a minor administrative event. But for you, it can be years of life, identity, effort, confusion, adjustment, and learning how to read rooms you were never fully invited into.

That’s what Accenture gave me.

Not just project experience.

Not just CRM, consent governance, LLM evaluation, or reporting.

It gave me a clearer understanding of how enterprise work can separate the person doing the work from the person buying the work.

It showed me that the buyer’s journey can disappear behind account structures, staffing systems, internal politics, and delivery layers.

It showed me that access can be formal but not useful.

A badge.

A laptop.

A title.

A Teams channel.

A Workday posting.

A project assignment.

All of that can be real access and still not be the access that changes your position.

Looking back, Accenture taught me that access to the work isn’t the same as access to the deal.

title: I Had the Keys, Not the Leverage
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...Not literally, but functionally.I was working at Saks OFF 5TH in Lincoln Park, and I was initially hired as an Operations Specialist. This was around March 2016.
html:
Last time...

Not literally, but functionally.

I was working at Saks OFF 5TH in Lincoln Park, and I was initially hired as an Operations Specialist. This was around March 2016. My shift started at 4:30 in the morning, which meant leaving from the South Side, biking or catching a bus to the Red Line, then riding north while most people were still asleep.

That alone made the job feel different.

Retail usually shows itself to the customer once the lights are on, the doors are open, the signage is placed, and the racks look halfway intentional. But somebody has to be there before that. Somebody has to receive the freight, break down the pallets, tag the product, fix the signage, process what didn’t get processed, and make the floor ready for the person who’s going to walk in later thinking they’re just browsing.

That was the part of the buyer’s journey I was closest to in Chicago.

Store readiness.

Before the customer could consider anything, the store had to be made consider-able.

At first, that meant being there with Diego, the key holder at the time. Some mornings, the whole first question was whether Diego was actually there. If he wasn’t, I was outside in whatever weather Chicago decided to be that day, waiting around with no real control over the situation. Sometimes Monica, the store leader, might be involved too. But the basic issue was simple: I could be responsible enough to show up at 4:30 a.m., but still not have the access needed to get inside.

That’s a specific kind of powerless.

Once the store got opened and activated, we’d head to the inventory room and start handling whatever had been left for us. Sometimes it was work from the early shift. Sometimes it was something left from later in the day. Then the doorbell would ring, which usually meant the shipment truck was downstairs.

We’d take the freight elevator down and start unloading with the pallet jack.

A standard shipment could be eight to ten pallets. On a slower inbound day, maybe three or four. Since this was Saks OFF 5TH, the product could be new merchandise, transfers from another store, or whatever came through that discounted Saks pipeline.

Ideally, the pallets were stacked and wrapped cleanly.

That didn’t always happen.

If the pallet was awkward, leaning, or shaped like somebody wrapped it with a grudge, getting it up the elevator was its own little game. Once it made it upstairs, we’d break it down by department. Men’s, women’s, kids, shoes, whatever it was. Then we’d stage it on fixtures so the morning associates could process it once they came in.

After shipment, there was always more.

Tagging. Ticketing. Adding stickers. Placing signage. Rearranging areas for promotions. Cleaning up whatever the sales day had left behind. Fixing things that hadn’t been processed correctly the first time.

Shoes were some of the worst.

Men’s, women’s, children’s. Mix-matched pairs. Stickers removed. Bottoms dirty because somebody tried them on and walked around like the store was their closet. And then you’d still have to deal with the SKU or UPC situation, trying to match the physical item back to whatever the system thought it was.

Department store inventory is its own kind of mythology.

I’m not saying that as a joke either. The taxonomy of a department store is always pretending to be more accurate than the floor allows it to be. Products move. Customers move them. Associates recover them. Tags get pulled. Stickers get switched. Boxes get separated from shoes. Systems say one thing, the floor says another, and the person doing inventory has to negotiate between both.

That was one side of the role.

The other side was access.

At the Lincoln Park store, there were maybe eight or nine registers. You accessed them with your associate ID. Once my operational duties were done, I could check customers out if needed, especially if another task had brought me toward the register area.

But the more interesting access issue was online fulfillment.

That workflow made the store feel like a warehouse hiding inside a sales floor.

You’d take an iPad and fulfill online orders from Saks or Saks OFF 5TH customers. The customer had already bought the item online. The store inventory had to satisfy the order. So now you were walking the floor like a fake personal shopper, finding items that were already paid for, removing security tags, boxing them, printing shipping labels with customer address information, and setting them aside for pickup.

I noticed the loss-prevention issue at the time.

If someone is pulling paid merchandise from the floor, removing the security tag, printing a label, and staging it somewhere, the audit trail needs to be clean. If there isn’t clear history around what label was printed, what order it belonged to, who handled it, and where the item went, that’s not just a process gap.

That’s an access gap.

Because from the outside, it might look like fulfillment.

From the inside, it’s also a path where merchandise can move out of the store with less friction than normal.

That didn’t mean everyone was doing something wrong. It meant the process depended on trust, tracking, and discipline. If any of those were loose, the risk was already there.

That’s where Saks started to connect back to the theme of this series.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing sales and sometimes supporting consideration.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was over, but the trust wasn’t.

At Trunk Club, the decision came back in a box.

At Saks in Chicago, the buyer wasn’t there yet, but the store still had to be made ready for them. The buyer’s journey was upstream from me, but everything I touched could affect whether that journey felt clean once they arrived.

Then came the key.

Diego eventually had to leave after a workplace incident involving comments he made. I’m not going to turn that into the center of this, but it changed the access reality inside the store.

Before or around that period, I’d been given a key.

So now I was a key holder.

Kind of.

I officially changed the title, but everything else mostly stayed the same. There wasn’t some major pay jump or grand repositioning. If there was an increase, it was probably a quarter or fifty cents, something funny like that. The real business need was simpler: somebody needed to be able to open the store when the truck got there.

Then I became a key holder in the most retail way possible.

The business needed someone reliable enough to open the door, but not enough to fully reposition me around the responsibility.

That’s the whole tension.

A key gives the appearance of authority, but it doesn’t automatically give leverage. It doesn’t let you make your own schedule. It doesn’t protect you from being left outside when somebody else is late. It doesn’t mean the business sees the responsibility the same way you feel it in your body at 4:30 in the morning.

It just means now you can get in.

Eventually, my life started moving in a different direction.

I was in a relationship with Brianna at the time, and we decided to move to Los Angeles. I’m grateful for that chapter, but it was also a mistake in the way certain life decisions can be both. You don’t always know what a move is going to cost until you’re already inside it.

I thought transferring to LA would mean transferring my role.

I figured I’d stay in operations, keep rocking, and just continue from another store.

That’s not what happened.

The transfer got approved, but the Beverly Connection store only had openings in Jewelry. Not operations. So I get to LA, go to the store to situate everything, and find out I need to re-interview with them.

That was my first clue that this wasn’t going to be a simple continuation.

The Beverly Connection store was across from the Beverly Center Macy’s, which is funny in hindsight because I moved out there with Brianna and ended up working near the kind of Los Angeles retail geography people only understand if they were really outside in it.

California also changed the structure around work.

Breaks, lunches, pay rules, the way time was treated, the whole thing felt different from Chicago. I’m not saying that from some legal analysis. I’m saying that as somebody who went from one retail environment into another and immediately felt the operating system had changed.

And then there was Jewelry.

That was a complete pivot.

In Chicago, I had freight elevators, pallets, inventory rooms, online fulfillment, bank deposits, register support, signage, promos, and operational routines. In LA, the buyer was right there.

No early-morning buffer.

No shipment work to hide inside.

No back-of-house rhythm I already understood.

Just the customer, the counter, the item, and the expectation that I’d sell.

Jewelry put me back into direct consideration and decision support. A customer looking at jewelry is usually weighing more than the object. They’re thinking about price, taste, occasion, gift value, status, how it looks, whether it feels cheap, whether it feels special, whether the person they’re buying it for might like it.

That’s a different kind of pressure than unloading a truck.

I can say I gained some social experience there. I gained some sales experience too, even if it was more tacit than formal. I was directly next to the customer in a way I hadn’t been in Chicago operations.

But I was also overwhelmed.

My personal life was loud at the time, and it bled into how I experienced the role. LA was a culture shock. The pace was different. The attitude was different. The utility of everything felt different. Even basic work expectations felt like they belonged to another script.

The management culture also felt clique-heavy in a way I didn’t know how to navigate. There were clear favorites, clear in-groups, and a social code I wasn’t fluent in.

That’s not unique to that store. Sales environments can get like that anywhere. But in LA, inside that specific department, while I was already dealing with a personal-life transition, it hit different.

They stayed on me about pants too, which was hilarious in its own way because this was still a discount store trying to act like the floor was Rodeo Drive.

At one point, somebody even gave me a card to go buy pants for a jewelry event because we were going to be in front of the “good people” and I needed to look the part.

I love that for me.

But that was also part of the role. Presentation mattered more in Jewelry. The look mattered. The department mattered. The buyer’s perception mattered. I’d come from operational usefulness, where the question was whether the truck got unloaded and the store got ready. Now the question was whether I looked and sounded like someone who belonged near the case.

That was a different kind of access.

In Chicago, I had access to the store before the buyer arrived.

In LA, I had access to the buyer without the operational authority I’d built my confidence around.

That’s the contrast.

Chicago gave me keys, registers, deposits, freight, fulfillment, and the feeling that I was trusted with the bones of the store, even if the leverage didn’t match.

LA put me closer to the buyer, but farther from the part of the business where I felt competent.

That’s why Saks belongs in this series.

It shows that being closer to the buyer isn’t always a promotion in practice. Sometimes it’s just a different exposure. A different risk. A different way to feel underprepared.

I didn’t make it a full year in that LA version before I pivoted to Vox DJs for the interim, then eventually decided to leave LA and come back to Chicago.

Looking back, Saks taught me a lot about access.

A key can open the door without changing your standing.

A register login can let you process a sale without giving you control over the sales environment.

An iPad can let you fulfill an online order without making the process secure.

A transfer can move you closer to the buyer while stripping away the part of the job that made you useful.

That’s what I understand now.

Saks taught me that access can put you inside the building before it gives you any real leverage inside the system.

Next in Series...

Connect with Me!

title: Setting Up OpenClaw, Part 11: Ambient Room Triage for Slack, X Links, and YouTube
author: Henry
