html:
Part 10 was about giving OpenClaw a Substack tool so an agent could help move writing into a publishing workflow.

This part is about a different kind of tool problem: what happens when the agent is sitting inside a live Slack room.

That sounds simple until it starts working.

If the agent only responds when I mention it, the behavior is predictable. I say something like:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
@WhiteClaw read this link and tell me what matters

The bot replies.

That is the normal chatbot pattern.

But OpenClaw can do something more interesting. It can listen to a room, treat unmentioned messages as room events, and decide whether a visible reply is useful.

That is the beginning of an ambient agent.

It is also where the setup gets more subtle.

An ambient Slack agent has to answer three questions on every message:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Should I respond at all?
If I respond, what source should I inspect first?
If I use tools, did I actually use the right ones?

The work from this setup session was about making those three questions explicit.

I call this pattern ambient room triage.

Ambient does not mean always talking

The first mistake is thinking ambient means "the bot replies to everything."

That is not what I want.

I want the agent to feel present in the room without turning the room into a bot transcript. Most messages should not get a visible reply. A link-only post may just be something I am saving for later. A screenshot may be obvious. A rant may not need the agent jumping in every time.

The useful behavior is more like:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
listen
understand the room context
stay quiet most of the time
reply when the reply adds real value

This is the difference between a chatbot and an ambient room agent.

A chatbot waits for a command.

An ambient room agent is allowed to notice.

But "allowed to notice" still needs configuration.

The three switches

In OpenClaw, ambient Slack behavior is not one switch.

There are three different surfaces that matter.

The first is the channel allowlist:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Is this Slack room enabled for the bot?

The second is mention gating:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Does this room require @mention before the agent is allowed to process a message?

The third is unmentioned inbound behavior:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
If an allowed room sends a message without a mention, should that be treated as a normal request or a quiet room event?

The shape I wanted was:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
most Slack rooms:
  require a mention

selected Slack rooms:
  allow unmentioned room events

That gives me a sane default.

The bot is not ambient everywhere. It is ambient only in the rooms where I want that behavior.

Conceptually, the config looks like this:

# ==================== JSON CODE ====================
{
  "*": {
    "enabled": true,
    "requireMention": true,
    "users": ["<my-user-id>"]
  },
  "<ambient-room-id>": {
    "enabled": true,
    "requireMention": false,
    "users": ["<my-user-id>"]
  }
}

The important detail is that Slack channel overrides should use channel IDs, not room names.

Room names are for humans.

Channel IDs are what the integration routes on.

So adding another ambient room is not "turn on #general." It is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
find the Slack channel ID
add an explicit channel override
set requireMention:false
restart or reload the gateway
verify the config

That is the durable version of the setup.

Room events are quieter than user requests

The other important setting is the inbound event kind.

For ambient rooms, unmentioned messages should be treated as room events:

# ==================== JSON CODE ====================
{
  "messages": {
    "groupChat": {
      "unmentionedInbound": "room_event"
    }
  }
}

That matters because a room event is not the same thing as a direct command.

If I tag the bot, I am asking for a response.

If I drop a link in the room, I may only be adding context.

The agent should be able to see the link without assuming it has to speak. That is the whole point of room-event mode.

The practical test is not "does the bot answer every ambient message?"

The practical test is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Does the agent receive enough context to make a good decision?
Does it stay silent when the message is not worth interrupting?
Does it reply when the room would actually benefit?

That is the bar.

Link previews are not evidence

The next issue showed up with links.

Slack unfurls are useful for humans. They are not enough for an agent.

If I post a YouTube link, Slack may show the title and thumbnail.

If I post an X link, Slack may show the tweet preview and maybe the beginning of the text.

That is not the same as reading the source.

The rule I wanted was:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Do not answer from the unfurl alone.
Use the proper tool for the source.
Then answer.

That became the core of the Slack link triage skill.

For YouTube, the rule is:

# ==================== BASH CODE ====================
summarize "<url>" --youtube auto --length short

If the room is just a link stream and the YouTube link is not worth interrupting, the agent should stay silent.

But if the agent decides a visible reply is useful, it should summarize the video first. It should not guess from the title.

That distinction is important.

The answer should come from the video transcript or summary, not from a Slack preview card.

X search is not the whole source

X links created the more interesting failure.

OpenClaw had an X-native search tool available through the xAI/Grok path. That was useful because X is often hard for normal web fetchers. A normal web search or scrape can miss the post, hit a login wall, or only see the public preview.

The right first move for an X status URL is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
use x_search on the exact post URL or status ID

That part worked.

The problem was the second hop.

The X post linked to a blog post. The agent used `x_search`, saw that the tweet was basically a teaser for a longer article, and then answered:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
the evidence is in the linked blog

That was not good enough.

The agent had found the blog link, but it had not read the blog.

That is a classic agent-tooling bug. The system has the right tool, the model uses it once, the tool result points to the next source, and then the model stops too early.

For source-aware triage, the rule has to be stronger:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
If x_search reveals an outbound source link, follow it.

The updated behavior is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
1. Use x_search on the exact X post.
2. If the post or thread links to a blog, paper, GitHub repo, docs page, video, or article, fetch that source.
3. Use web_fetch first.
4. If web_fetch is thin, blocked, or incomplete, use Firecrawl as a fallback.
5. Only then judge evidence, credibility, or usefulness.

The most important sentence in the instruction is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Do not say "the evidence is in the linked blog" unless you tried to read it and could not.

That is the difference between a shallow link reaction and actual source-aware triage.

Skills are not always enough

The first version of the fix lived in a skill file.

That was directionally right. A reusable skill is the correct place for this kind of behavior:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Slack link appears
  -> decide whether to reply
  -> pick the source-specific tool
  -> read the source
  -> answer concisely

But the actual Slack run exposed a prompt-loading detail.

The skill was visible to the agent as a compact skill entry, but the full body of the skill was not necessarily injected into every Slack turn. In the real failure case, the agent saw enough to know `x_search` existed, but it did not reliably follow the detailed second-hop rule from the skill.

The fix was to move the critical rule into the always-loaded workspace instructions.

That made the rule impossible to miss:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
For X/Twitter status URLs, use x_search first.
If x_search reveals an outbound source link, fetch it before judging the post.
If web_fetch is incomplete, try Firecrawl.
Answer from both the post and the linked source.

The skill still matters.

But the highest-priority behavioral rule belongs somewhere the agent sees on every relevant turn.

That is a practical lesson for OpenClaw setups:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Put reusable workflows in skills.
Put must-not-miss safety or quality rules in always-loaded instructions.

The trace is the truth

The visible Slack answer made the problem obvious, but the trace proved it.

The bad answer said the linked blog supposedly contained the evidence.

That sounded like the agent had not read it.

Instead of guessing, I checked the OpenClaw session trace.

The trace showed one tool call:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
x_search

It did not show:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
web_fetch
firecrawl_scrape

That settled it.

The agent had not read the linked article.

This is one of the best things about running a local agent gateway. You do not have to infer everything from the chat bubble. You can inspect the session.

The useful debugging commands are conceptually:

# ==================== BASH CODE ====================
openclaw sessions list --json
openclaw sessions tail --session-key "<session-key>" --tail 80
openclaw sessions export-trajectory --session-key "<session-key>" --workspace "<workspace>" --json

The session tail shows the timeline.

The trajectory export shows the tool calls, tool results, prompts, and final answer.

That is how I confirmed the failure mode:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
not a Slack delivery problem
not an X auth problem
not a Firecrawl problem
not a model refusal

the model stopped after x_search

Once you know that, the fix is straightforward.

A good diagnostic uses the same wording

After changing the instruction, I did not test with an idealized prompt.

I tested with the same style of request that caused the miss:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
use x_search on this X post and tell me:
1. what the claim is
2. whether the thread gives evidence
3. what I should pay attention to

That wording matters because the original user instruction said `x_search`.

A weaker agent might treat that as permission to only use `x_search`.

The better behavior is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Use x_search as the first tool.
Then follow the source links that x_search discovers.

The successful diagnostic showed the right tool chain:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
x_search
web_fetch
firecrawl_scrape

And the answer changed.

Instead of saying "the evidence is in the linked blog," it summarized what the linked blog actually supported.

That is the point of the fix.

Not "use more tools."

Use the next source.

Images and screenshots are part of the room too

The other practical detail is that Slack rooms are not just text.

I post screenshots, charts, tweet screenshots, memes, images, and videos. For an ambient room agent to feel natural, it has to treat those as first-class room context.

OpenClaw was already passing media into the agent turn when Slack delivered it. The session metadata showed image events and media attachments, and the model calls had image understanding enabled.

That means the agent can often inspect screenshots directly.

The best practice is still simple:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
If I want a specific answer, tag the bot in the same message as the image.

Posting an image first and tagging the bot in the next message can work if the prior image is still in the assembled context, but it is less reliable.

For screenshots with tiny text, I should expect normal OCR limits. If the exact words matter, paste the link or the key text too.

The important mental model is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Slack message text
Slack file attachments
Slack unfurls
recent room context
tool results

These are all separate sources.

A good agent learns which one is authoritative for the task.

OpenClaw's built-in web tools stay primary

Another clarification from this setup was tool priority.

I do not want every web task to go straight to an external search provider just because one is installed.

OpenClaw already has its own web search and fetch surface. Firecrawl and Exa are useful, but they should be extra tools, not the default answer to everything.

The order I want is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
normal web page:
  web_fetch first
  Firecrawl if the page is thin, blocked, or JavaScript-heavy
  search only when the URL is not enough

X/Twitter post:
  x_search first
  then fetch outbound links

YouTube:
  summarize CLI first

broader research:
  web_search, Firecrawl search, Exa, or browser depending on the job

This makes the system easier to reason about.

The agent is not "searching the web" in a generic way.

It is routing the source to the best reader.

The final room setup

After the link triage fix, I expanded the ambient room set.

The default remains conservative:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
all other Slack rooms:
  require mention

Then I added a small number of rooms where unmentioned room events are useful:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
selected rooms:
  requireMention:false
  unmentioned inbound handled as room_event

This is the setup I want because it matches how I actually use Slack.

Some rooms are working surfaces. I want the agent to feel present there.

Other rooms are just places where the bot should answer when called.

The distinction matters more than the exact number of rooms.

An ambient agent should be configured room by room, not globally unleashed.

The operating loop

The finished loop looks like this:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
Slack room chatter comes in.

If the room is not ambient:
  wait for mention.

If the room is ambient:
  treat unmentioned chatter as room context.

If the message contains a YouTube link:
  summarize the video before replying.

If the message contains an X link:
  use x_search first.
  then fetch the outbound source if there is one.

If the message contains an image:
  inspect the image when it is relevant.

If the message is not worth interrupting:
  stay silent.

That is the behavior I was trying to get.

The key is not one tool or one config flag. It is the combination:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
room-level ambient permissions
quiet room-event handling
source-specific link readers
visible reply restraint
session trace debugging
always-loaded quality rules

That combination is what makes the agent feel natural.

The lesson

The lesson from this setup is that ambient agents need triage.

Without triage, they either do too little or too much.

Too little:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
The agent sees a link preview and gives a shallow answer.

Too much:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
The agent replies to every room message and becomes noise.

The better pattern is:

# ==================== TEXT CODE ====================
listen broadly
answer selectively
read primary sources
verify tool usage
keep defaults conservative
make ambient behavior explicit room by room

That is why I think "ambient room triage" is the right name for this layer of the setup.

It is not just Slack configuration.

It is the part of the agent system that decides when a room message deserves work, what source should be trusted, and whether the answer should become visible.

That is the difference between a bot that sits in a room and an agent that can actually participate in one.

title: The Decision Came Back in a Box
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...Like the harbor job, I found it on Craigslist. That pattern mattered because I was still learning how to find my own exits. Levi’s had been inconsistent. The harbor had been seasonal.
html:
Last time...

Like the harbor job, I found it on Craigslist. That pattern mattered because I was still learning how to find my own exits. Levi’s had been inconsistent. The harbor had been seasonal. Trunk Club felt like the next door opening.

And I was excited enough about it to tell a few people still at Levi’s that this was the wave and they should come get some money too.

At least three people came through that gateway. Through them, who knows. But it was a gateway for sure.

This was February 2015 to March 2016. My title was Operations Associate, but the role had two lives. I started in inventory. I finished in operations.

Trunk Club still had that startup energy where everything felt impressive, improvised, and a little fly-by-night at the same time. The warehouse was on Goose Island, but the company also had the Ohio Street location downtown, the swanky brick-and-mortar setup where customers could have the try-on experience in person. That side had the rooftop, the polish, the brand environment.

The warehouse had the process.

Inventory was where I started.

We were a team of around eight, and a lot of the work came from items that had already gone through the customer. A customer had received a trunk, tried things on, kept what they wanted, rejected what they didn’t, and sent the rest back. Sometimes it was a clean rejection. Sometimes it was a return after more use. Either way, the decision came back into the building as product.

That’s where we came in.

Items had to be evaluated. Some needed dry cleaning. Some needed steaming. Some needed to be re-tagged. Some were too far gone and had to be damaged out.

Shoes were their own little world.

A lot of them were Cole Haans, Hamiltons, dress shoes, and Chelsea boots before Chelsea boots got run into the ground. If shoes came back looking rough, we’d shoe-horn them and hit them with heat guns to try to recapture the shape. Some customers were clearly trying to juug the process, so the item had to tell the truth even if the customer didn’t.

Then we’d notate the shoe, the model, the condition, and what we’d done with it.

I’d switch tasks sometimes and steam collared shirts or other items that needed it. We also had to look up products in the internal inventory system, and sometimes I think through Trunk Club’s public site, so we could find the SKU, print it, and re-tag the item correctly.

The work wasn’t hard.

It was easy in the way tedious work can be easy, where your brain knows what to do but the shift still moves slow.

That was the first half of Trunk Club for me. Returned product. Condition checks. SKU lookups. Re-tagging. Steaming. Heat guns. Shoes that needed to be saved if they could be saved. Items that had already been considered, tried, denied, or returned.

Looking at it through the buyer’s journey, I wasn’t near the buyer directly anymore.

But I was near the evidence of their decision.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing sales and sometimes supporting consideration.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was over, but trust still had to be maintained.

At Trunk Club, the customer’s decision came back in a box.

That box carried data, inventory, condition, preference, rejection, and future sales potential. If the item came back and got processed wrong, the next customer experience could be affected. If the SKU was wrong, if the item wasn’t cleaned, if the shoe shape wasn’t restored, if damaged inventory stayed in circulation, the personalized commerce model got weaker.

So even though I wasn’t selling, I was inside the operational layer that made the selling model possible.

After a few months, I wanted to move departments.

Inventory was fine, but it was slow. Operations had more motion, more hours, more music, more people I knew, and more of the late-shift warehouse energy I wanted to be around.

The operations shift came in around 5 p.m. and could go until 10 p.m. or later. There were day operations people too, but the evening shift had a different feel. Music was playing over the warehouse speakers. The homies were there. The managers were cooler. Edwin was cool as hell. Breaks could turn into shenanigans. It had more life to it.

My supervisor Karen pushed back on the move, which I didn’t fully clock then, but later understood as a red flag.

Eventually, I got approved and moved over to operations under Joe.

Joe was cool.

Operations was the iPad-cart side of the business.

You’d take a cart with a basket, and the iPad was mounted on it. You’d log into your profile, pull up the portal, switch it to picking, and start walking the warehouse floor for selections that needed to be fulfilled.

The warehouse had sections. Shoes, coats, shirts, and whatever else. The system didn’t give me some perfectly routed path. You had to know the floor well enough to find what you needed.

If you had to grab 30 items, that was timed.

Your profile tracked the work. Leadership could see it. You could see your own time. The whole thing was measured and gamified enough to make late-shift warehouse people want to be on their shit. There were contests, praise, food, money, and of course free social pressure.

That was the work becoming data.

The other half was packing.

Someone would take the cubbies or containers filled with fulfilled orders to a pack station. That station had a PC and a little label printer. From there, the trunk had to be packed efficiently and correctly. Sometimes that meant actual trunk-like containers. Sometimes it meant branded shipping boxes. Either way, the packing had to match the stylist/customer selections before the order got sealed.

Then the trunks were arranged on the floor, set onto pallets, wrapped, and moved to the bay area to be picked up and loaded onto a truck later.

Some people were designated to build pallets. I think I did it a few times. There was also someone designated to deal with the trash, break everything down, and dispose of it.

Picking was more fun than packing.

Packing was still cool, but picking had more motion. A cart, a login, a timer, a warehouse path, a little pressure, and the music carrying the shift.

That’s where the access lesson showed up.

I had a login, a cart, a timer, and a path through the warehouse. That didn’t mean I had authority. It meant my access had become measurable.

That was different from the earlier jobs.

At O’Brien’s, access was mostly physical and task-based.

At Macy’s, I had POS access but limited authority.

At Levi’s, I had access to fitting rooms, inventory areas, and the customer’s moment of consideration without much control over the close.

At DuSable Harbor, low-ranking access got heavier because it touched gates, payments, customer profiles, and physical infrastructure.

At Trunk Club, access became tracked.

The system knew who was picking. It knew how long it took. It knew what profile the work was under. It knew whether the fulfillment process was moving or dragging.

I wasn’t designing the process. I wasn’t choosing the customer’s wardrobe. I wasn’t building the business strategy. I wasn’t managing the KPI model.

I was just inside it.

And that was enough to see something.

The buyer’s journey doesn’t disappear after the customer clicks, rejects, keeps, or returns something. It turns into work somewhere else.

It becomes inventory.

It becomes a SKU.

It becomes a damaged-out item.

It becomes a heat-gunned shoe.

It becomes a timed pick.

It becomes a packed trunk.

It becomes a metric under somebody’s profile.

That’s what Trunk Club showed me.

The customer wasn’t in front of me anymore, but their choices were still moving through the warehouse.

The decision came back in a box, and my job was to help the system decide what happened to it next.

Next in Series...

Connect with Me!

title: The Sale Was Over, But the Trust Wasn’t
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...More specifically, I found a dock worker role with Suntex at DuSable Harbor.
html:
Last time...

More specifically, I found a dock worker role with Suntex at DuSable Harbor. This was around June 2014 to February 2015, and I found the job on Craigslist.

That alone felt like something.

Levi’s had me sitting around too often, waiting to see if I’d get scheduled, called in, or given a short closing shift that barely made the commute feel worth it. Finding the harbor job made me two-job shawty for a minute, which felt better than sitting at home hoping Levi’s would call me in.

It was outside my comfort zone, but not in the same way retail had been.

At Levi’s, the discomfort came from having to perform styling and sales energy on demand. At the harbor, the work was more physical, more environmental, and more service-based. Put the shirt on, be identifiable, be available, and handle what needed to be handled.

A morning could start with turning on the two checkout desk computers. Ideally, the manager had already lifted the store guard. Then there were the public restrooms, male and female, which had to be cleaned and replenished. The front desk had shelves in front of it with snacks, drinks, Dramamine, and basic items people could buy. Behind that was the manager’s office and a utility closet.

During boating season, the work moved around.

We’d help boaters with mooring and departures. We’d walk the docks to see if anybody needed anything. We’d keep the grounds clean, the parking lot clean, and the dock waters clear of excess trash or dead fish. We’d help refill the drink cooler or stock the shelves if nobody else had jumped on it. Sometimes there were meter readings or audits on dock boxes.

A customer could be someone who actually docked with us. It could be someone settling an unpaid balance, slip fee, fuel charge, or general account issue. It could be somebody who just stopped in and wanted a drink or a snack. At peak season, there was a mix of boat owners, guests, tourists, and random walk-ins. As the season slowed down, it was more boaters, randoms settling things, and eventually just randoms.

So the buyer’s journey was different again.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was processing sales and sometimes supporting consideration.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still trying things on.

At DuSable Harbor, the sale was mostly over.

A lot of the real work sat after the purchase decision. Someone had already chosen the harbor, already had a slip, already trusted the place with their boat, or already walked in expecting the basics to work. My job wasn’t to convince them to buy into the harbor. My job was to help maintain the environment that made their decision feel stable.

That’s where trust lived.

In the bathroom being clean.

In the docks being walkable.

In somebody being around if a boater needed help.

In the gate code working.

In the grounds not looking neglected.

In the front desk being able to pull up a customer profile or take a payment without making the interaction harder than it needed to be.

The access was heavier than the title made it sound.

I was still a go-for, but this time I had access to more consequential things. I had dock gate codes that changed each season. I had access to the desk computers. I could pull up customer profiles. If someone needed to settle something or update their information, I could help bring up their account. I could manually enter bare credit cards into the same general area where we’d ring up a candy bar.

That’s wild to think about now.

A low-ranking worker could be cleaning a restroom, refilling a cooler, walking a dock, and then handling someone’s payment information in the same shift.

That’s an access lesson.

DuSable Harbor taught me that low-ranking workers can still hold high-risk access.

Not glamorous access. Not executive access. Not the kind of access people write strategy decks about. But real access.

Physical access.

Customer access.

Payment access.

Gate access.

Environmental access.

The kind of access that matters because something can go wrong if the person holding it doesn’t understand the weight of it.

I had access to the docks through the gate codes. I had access to utility carts to move around the grounds. I never operated the small speed boat myself, but I did accompany managers and other dockhands when a circumstance required it. I had access to the fitting-room equivalent of the marina, meaning the behind-the-scenes areas customers didn’t fully see but depended on anyway.

But I didn’t have much authority.

I couldn’t make my own schedule. I had a uniform. I had expectations around how I was supposed to look, where I was supposed to be, and what I was supposed to do. I was basically a go-for again, just in a different environment.

The uniform was its own constraint too.

The city-provided blue shirt didn’t have much life to it, and the khaki expectation felt like it came from somebody else’s idea of neutral. I had my own shorts I preferred, and I wasn’t exactly building my wardrobe around harbor khaki compliance. That was always a thing.

The environment had another layer I didn’t have language for at the time.

A lot of the work placed me in service to people whose leisure looked very different from my life. This was the dock next to Navy Pier. The boats, the slips, the casual way people moved through that space, it was a whole world I hadn’t really been around before.

I didn’t know anything nautical before that job, so even the basic parts of the work gave me exposure I wouldn’t have gotten otherwise.

That part was useful.

The job helped get me out of my shell a bit more too, but not through retail performance. More through proximity. You’re in the shirt. You’re on the dock. Somebody needs something. You figure out how to respond.

There were characters among the other dockhands. Some still exist somewhere in the Facebook layer of life, but that’s really it. There was also workplace messiness around management and staff that reminded me I was seeing only one layer of the operation. I didn’t know what was true, what was rumor, or what had been handled above me. I just knew the environment had its own politics, and I was still low on the ladder.

When the season ended, they tried to have some of us convert into helping set up the Millennium Park ice skating rink.

I did it for a few days.

But by then, the job felt like it had become something else. The hours, the pay, the cold, the new supervisors, the unfamiliar grizzly energy around January and February, none of it felt like the move. Whatever made sense during boating season felt dead by winter.

So I started looking for another way.

Eventually, that led me to Trunk Club.

Looking back, DuSable Harbor wasn’t a buyer’s journey lesson in the traditional sales sense. It was more of a customer journey lesson. The customer had already bought in, docked, arrived, or trusted the place enough to hand over payment information.

The question was what happened after that.

Was the harbor clean?

Was the dock accessible?

Was the person at the desk competent?

Was the payment handled correctly?

Was the environment being watched?

Was the basic trust of the place being maintained?

That’s what the job showed me.

The sale can be over, but the trust isn’t.

title: The Buyer Was Still Trying Things On
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...A lot of the time, they were still trying things on.I worked at the Levi’s flagship on Michigan Avenue from September 2013 to May 2014.
html:
Last time...

A lot of the time, they were still trying things on.

I worked at the Levi’s flagship on Michigan Avenue from September 2013 to May 2014. My title was Stylist, which sounded cleaner than the role felt while I was inside of it.

On paper, it was about impacting customer shopping habits, helping drive sales through personal connections, maintaining the floor, developing personal sales strategies, and supporting store goals during peak seasons.

In reality, I was still figuring out whether I was even built for that kind of selling yet.

I liked clothes. I liked fashion. I liked denim, jackets, shirts, and the way a fit could change how someone carried themselves. That part made sense to me.

What didn’t come naturally was approaching strangers, building rapport on demand, and turning product knowledge into a conversation that moved somebody closer to buying.

That gap followed me into the role.

I’d come out of Macy’s with enough retail experience to know I wanted something different, or at least something more specific. I remember searching Craigslist and the Levi’s website, trying to find a way in. The job was a pain to get.

The interview was a group interview. Matt Hambric was there, and so was this dude named Adam. I didn’t know how to prepare for interviews then, so I walked in with personality and hope. I remember saying something to Adam that probably showed the wrong kind of curiosity for the room. Matt vouched for me in a way that kept me alive in the process.

Matt was one of those people I’d call a brother in the familiar sense, not blood, but familiar. Fellow Ogden and Lincoln Park connection. Someone who understood me enough in that moment to not let one awkward turn define me.

That mattered.

Once I got the role, though, the title didn’t solve the actual work.

Levi’s had real product knowledge. Fits mattered. A 501 wasn’t the same conversation as a 511, 510, or 514. Wash mattered. Size mattered. Some customers came in knowing exactly what they wanted. Some came in asking for a specific cut or stone wash. Some were tourists who wanted to experience the flagship because of the brand and store history. Some needed more personal help.

That’s where the buyer’s journey was different.

At O’Brien’s, the buyer had already decided.

At Macy’s, I was often processing a sale that was already in motion.

At Levi’s, the buyer was still in consideration.

They might’ve liked the brand but not known the fit. They might’ve known the fit but not the wash. They might’ve walked into the fitting room with five options and come out liking none of them. The sale was still open. The decision could still move.

Styling, when done well, is guided consideration.

It’s not just telling someone what looks good. It’s helping them interpret what they’re already reacting to. Too tight. Too loose. Too stiff. Too plain. Too trendy. Too expensive. Too different from what they normally wear. Too close to what they already own.

The fitting room becomes the real sales floor because that’s where the buyer starts telling the truth with their body language.

I understood pieces of that, but I wasn’t consistent yet.

If my energy was on, or if the customer had a complementary energy that helped cover my shortcomings, I could be useful. I could speak better to a cut I knew. I could help someone think through a pair of jeans or a jacket. I could be present enough to make the interaction easier.

But if I wasn’t on, the role felt harder than the title made it sound.

A lot of the default work was recovery. Opening fitting rooms. Running sizes if someone asked. Cleaning up what came out of the rooms. Refilling fixtures. Making sure items were sized properly. Fixing displays. Greeting people at the front.

Greeting had another layer too. On Michigan Avenue, the front of the store wasn’t just a welcome point. It was also a soft loss prevention position. Tourists, shoppers, people passing through, people who might buy, people who might snatch and grab. You were part of the atmosphere and part of the watch.

So again, access had layers.

I had access to the store once it was open. I had access to the fitting rooms and the keys. I had access to bathrooms, the back office area, the inventory area, the break room upstairs that doubled as storage for mannequins, banners, and whatever else needed somewhere to go.

But I only had authority over myself.

Even the register was different from Macy’s. At Macy’s, registers were spread out across departments, and associates could unlock a POS with their own ID. At Levi’s, the register area was more centralized, one long block of terminals. You had to make sure the customer knew your name so whoever was ringing them up could enter your associate number and credit you properly.

That says a lot about the role.

You could help influence the decision, but someone else might finalize the transaction. You could spend time with the customer, but the credit still had to be captured correctly. You could be close to the sale without fully owning the close.

And even then, the role was hard to build momentum in because I was seldom scheduled.

Sometimes I was on-call. Sometimes I was off. Sometimes I came in for a short three-hour closing shift. It’s hard to develop rhythm in a role when most of your shifts are on-call, short closing shifts, or dependent on someone else calling off.

That was frustrating.

Not in some abstract professional-development way. In a real way. I wasn’t making money sitting at home hoping another person didn’t come in. I didn’t know how to apply myself better inside the situation, so it felt like being trapped inside something I’d signed up for.

That’s a strange feeling.

Wanting the job. Getting the job. Then realizing the job doesn’t actually give you enough room to become good at it or enough hours to make it make sense.

The main value ended up being the people.

Levi’s put me around people I may not have met otherwise. Some of those connections lasted longer than the job. And that matters too, because sometimes a role doesn’t give you the career lesson you expected. Sometimes it gives you the people, the environment, and the discomfort that help you understand what you need next.

Eventually, I found the docks. Then from there, I found Trunk Club.

When I finally had other sources, it felt good to leave Levi’s where I found it.

Looking back, Levi’s didn’t make me a great stylist. It showed me what styling was supposed to require.

Product knowledge wasn’t enough.

Access to the fitting room wasn’t enough.

A title wasn’t enough.

The buyer was still trying things on, and I was still trying to understand what kind of support a person needs before they can guide someone else with confidence.

title: AI Governance Without Ratification Is Just Wishful Thinking
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...A company says a tool will improve internal communication. A vendor says their platform will centralize decision-making.
html:
Last time...

A company says a tool will improve internal communication. A vendor says their platform will centralize decision-making. A team says the new system will create transparency, accountability, and better collaboration.

Maybe it will.

But maybe the real conversations still happen in Teams. Maybe the actual approvals still happen over email. Maybe the urgent context still lives in someone’s DMs. Maybe the product of record is technically available, but the business is still operating through side channels because that is where people already know how to move.

That’s where AI governance starts to get interesting.

Not at the point where someone buys the tool. Not even at the point where someone writes the policy. The real question is whether the intended behavior has been ratified by reality.

If the system is supposed to improve communication, are people actually communicating there?

If the tool is supposed to create visibility, can leaders actually see what matters inside it?

If the workflow is supposed to reduce risk, is the risky behavior actually being redirected, or has it just moved into a less visible channel?

This is the difference between implementation and ratification.

Implementation says, “We launched it.”

Ratification asks, “Did the business actually absorb it?”

That distinction matters even more with AI because AI does not just create new outputs. It changes where decisions are made, who gets influence, what gets documented, and what can be quietly skipped.

A company can say it has an AI governance process. But if employees are pasting sensitive context into unmanaged tools because the approved process is too slow, the governance is not functioning. A company can say it has a central platform for collaboration. But if key decisions still happen in email threads and chat messages outside that platform, the source of truth is fractured.

That is not just an operations issue.

That is a cyber issue.

Access, communication, and governance are connected. If the wrong people can access the right information in the wrong place, the business has a control problem. If the right people cannot find the right information in the approved place, the business has an adoption problem. If nobody is checking the difference, the business has a ratification problem.

This’s where companies fool themselves. They confuse availability with usage. They confuse policy with practice. They confuse “we have a tool for that” with “the work actually happens there.” AI governance cannot survive on that kind of wishful thinking.

Ratification is the missing layer. It is the act of proving that the intended behavior is happening, that the right people are accountable, and that the tool or process is not just sitting there as a decorative control.

A practical ratification check might ask:

  • Where does this communication actually happen today?

  • Where is it supposed to happen?

  • Who owns the gap between those two realities?

  • What evidence proves the workflow is being used?

  • What decisions are still happening outside the approved system?

  • Who has access to the tool, the data, and the exceptions?

  • When was the last time this process was tested against real behavior?

Those questions are not pedantic. They are the difference between governance as a slide and governance as an operating discipline.

The future of AI governance will not be won by the company with the longest policy document or the flashiest internal platform. It will be won by the companies willing to verify whether their own claims are true.

Because if the tool says one thing, the policy says another, and the people are working somewhere else entirely, the company does not have governance.

It has a wish…

title: Processing the Sale Is Not the Same as Making It
author: Diamond
excerpt: Last time...This was October 2012 to August 2013, at the Macy’s on State Street in Chicago. I was a sales associate, mostly in men’s apparel, often somewhere around Nautica.
html:
Last time...

This was October 2012 to August 2013, at the Macy’s on State Street in Chicago. I was a sales associate, mostly in men’s apparel, often somewhere around Nautica. I was still in high school, working part-time shifts, and probably wore a full suit to the interview, which says a lot.

I was serious, but green.

On paper, the role sounds clean enough.

  • Impact the customer shopping experience through in-store connections

  • Maintain the assigned floor area

  • Meet the daily personal sales goal

In practice, I was learning that being in a sales role and knowing how to sell are not the same thing.

The more tenured associates already had their own reality. Some had regulars. Some knew how to make a sale. Some understood the floor, the rhythm, the customers, and the quiet ways people move through a department store when they are deciding whether to buy something.

I didn’t have that yet.

A lot of my shifts were closer to standing in my assigned section, checking out customers who came by with merchandise, helping someone get into a fitting room, pointing them toward the right area, or offering advice when I had enough context to be useful.

That was still customer-facing work.

It just was not always the same as driving the sale.

Looking back through the buyer’s journey, Macy’s was different from O’Brien’s because the buyer was still deciding. They were browsing. They were checking sizes, comparing price tags, walking in and out of fitting rooms, asking where something was, or carrying items from another section because they just needed a register.

Some customers were in consideration.

Some were already at decision.

Most of the time, I was meeting them wherever they happened to be, without fully understanding how to move them from one stage to the next.

That is the honest version.

I was not building demand. I was not working a book of regular customers. I was not shaping vendor decisions or merchandise strategy. I was mostly reacting to buyer intent that was already in motion.

If somebody came to the register, I could process the sale.

If somebody needed a fitting room, I could help with that.

If somebody asked where something was, I could try to guide them.

If somebody needed a price checked, I could try to solve it without making the interaction harder than it needed to be.

That last part is where the access lesson gets interesting.

At Macy’s, every associate had an ID to unlock the POS system. So I had access to the register. I had access to the building through the Randolph Street employee entrance. I had access to multiple floors of merchandise. In certain sections, I could access fitting rooms. I had enough system access to help a customer move through the purchase.

But access is not the same as authority.

I remember learning that the hard way with price adjustments. The way it was explained to me, if a customer said an item was discounted, you could walk over, verify it, and if the scan did not reflect the correct price, adjust it to accommodate the customer. Functionally, the system allowed it.

So I did that.

Then it became a problem.

The assumption was that I may have been adjusting a price for someone I knew, when in reality this was a stranger. From my side, I thought I was doing what I had been told was part of helping the customer. From the business side, the action carried risk.

That is the gap.

A system can let you do something before the organization fully trusts your judgment doing it.

At the time, I would not have called that identity access management. I would have just called it getting in trouble for some bullshit.

But with more distance, I can see the lesson better.

Permissions, judgment, training, and trust all have to line up. If they don’t, the person closest to the customer can end up holding the confusion.

There was another layer too. My supervisor tried to walk the floor with me and practice basic engagement. “Pretend I’m a customer,” that kind of thing.

At that age, mock anything felt painful.

I was more socially acclimated than I had been at 15, but I was still introverted. I was not naturally open or outgoing enough at that time to be successful in the role at a base personality level. So the sales training felt misplaced, and honestly, me wanting a sales role at that time may have been misplaced too.

Needed $$$

That does not mean the job taught me nothing.

It taught me the difference between being near a transaction and understanding a sale.

It taught me that a buyer can be physically in front of you and still be in different stages mentally. One person needs help deciding. Another person only needs speed. Another person wants reassurance. Another person wants to be left alone until they are ready.

It also taught me that retail access is layered. You can enter the building, unlock the register, touch the merchandise, support the fitting room, and still have very little authority inside the actual business.

Macy’s made me visible to the customer before it made me powerful inside the operation.

That is probably the part I understand better now.

I was close enough to see the buyer deciding, but not developed enough yet to consistently influence the decision.

Most days, I was processing the sale.

I was still learning what it meant to make one.

title: The Buyer Had Already Decided
author: Diamond
excerpt: O’Brien’s Chicago IAMIt was around 2009, through O’Brien’s Chicago. I was about 15, and the opportunity came through an elementary school friend.
html:
It was around 2009, through O’Brien’s Chicago. I was about 15, and the opportunity came through an elementary school friend. I cannot say with certainty which event it was tied to, but it felt more like pop-up or festival service than me being a formal server inside the restaurant.

On an old resume, I called it food server experience.

That is technically true enough, but the memory is more specific than that.

I was running plates, spot-serving where I could, and mostly doing what I was asked to do. I was introverted, overwhelmed, and trying to be useful without fully knowing the flow yet. I wanted to start working, so I raised my hand. Once I was there, I felt more like a go-for than somebody with any real independence.

Looking at it now through the buyer’s journey, I was not shaping much of the buyer’s thinking.

The customer was already there. They were already hungry, already in motion, already inside whatever decision had brought them to that food line or service moment. By the time I touched the experience, the buyer had mostly moved past awareness and consideration.

They were in the decision moment, or maybe even slightly after it.

That is where I was.

Not creating demand. Not explaining options. Not guiding a choice in any meaningful way. More so helping the business keep up after the buyer had already decided to engage.

That is still part of the buyer experience, though.

If the plate is late, cold, wrong, missing something, or handed off poorly, the buyer does not separate that from the brand. They may not know who made the mistake. They may not care. To them, the experience is the experience.

That was probably one of my earliest lessons in being close to the buyer without owning the buyer relationship.

There is an access management thread in that too, even if it was not digital.

I had access to parts of the service flow. Plates, trays, food movement, instructions, back-and-forth communication, and the physical space where the customer experience was being fulfilled.

But I did not have authority over the actual offer.

I was not setting the menu. I was not pricing anything. I was not deciding how the event should be staffed. I was not responsible for why a customer chose O’Brien’s in the first place.

I had access to help move the process, but not enough authority to define the process.

That distinction has followed me into more mature work.

Sometimes you are near the buyer, but not moving the buyer. Sometimes you are trusted with part of the experience, but not the whole relationship. Sometimes the work is not persuasion at all. It is fulfillment under pressure.

O’Brien’s was that kind of lesson.

The buyer had already decided, and my job was to help make sure the decision still felt like a good one once the plate reached their hands.

title: The Two Riders: A Parable of Known and Unknowable Risk
author: Diamond
excerpt: The First Rider wore no helmet 殺She placed large headphones over her ears, blocking the sound of traffic At a wide intersection, she ignored the crosswalk and the signal, choosing instead to pedal...
html:
The First Rider wore no helmet 🚫🪖

She placed large headphones over her ears, blocking the sound of traffic 🎧

At a wide intersection, she ignored the crosswalk and the signal, choosing instead to pedal diagonally across four active lanes 🛣️

She cut directly through a truck’s blind spot as the driver made a legal left turn.

When the truck struck her and she tumbled to the ground, she immediately gestured at the driver in anger, as if the collision were entirely his fault 🖕🖕🖕

The First Rider did not suffer from bad luck. She suffered from a refusal to know. Every fact she needed, the physics of the truck, the geometry of the blind spot, the flow of traffic, was already knowable. She had not merely taken a risk; she had systematically eliminated every safer alternative. By removing her helmet, blocking her hearing, and ignoring the visible dangers around her, she chose by default the most dangerous path available. Even if the law had granted her the right of way, she had already gambled everything she could not afford to lose 🎰🎰🎰

The Second Rider did the opposite. She owned a well-built scooter from a reputable maker, maintained it carefully, and always wore a helmet. She rode on the park path rather than the street, followed every safety guideline, and kept her senses sharp. Yet one afternoon, the path concealed a small, uneven ridge, barely visible and completely outside her control. The wheel caught. She went over the handlebars and crashed hard 😵

The Second Rider had done nothing wrong, but the environment contained a flaw she could not have seen. This was not a failure of preparation; it was the remnant of risk that remains even when all personal controls are correct.

The Rub

The lesson for those steering large systems is this: most organizations are not choosing between being the First Rider or the Second Rider. They are doing both #atscale.

They send out fleets. Some riders are dispatched without helmets into blind spots, ignoring years of accumulated complexity because they treat a transformative force as if it were just another routine trip. Meanwhile, even the careful riders travel across an infrastructure full of hidden snags like decades of uneven pavement, undocumented corners, and masked/buried fragility. When one person crashes, you notice. When a tenth of the fleet crashes simultaneously across different times, places, and conditions, leadership may have no visibility into the scope of the failure. And if you cannot see the crashes, you cannot account for them in your plans.

The risk you take by refusing to know is yours.

The risk hidden in the pavement belongs to the system.

Sending out more riders without addressing both is simply wagering that no one will notice when the wheels finally catch.

Thanks for reading! This post is public so feel free to share it.

title: AI Is Not “Artificial Intelligence”, It’s Ambiguous Intelligence
author: Diamond
excerpt: Not because the tools are useless.Not because the technology is fake.But because the business often cannot clearly explain what the system knows, where it learned it, who shaped the inputs, who...
html:
Not because the tools are useless.

Not because the technology is fake.

But because the business often cannot clearly explain what the system knows, where it learned it, who shaped the inputs, who approved the outputs, or what happens when the result is wrong. Everybody just starts looking at one another.

That ambiguity is the real risk.

Most software tools do something specific.

A CRM stores customer records.

A billing system generates invoices.

A ticketing system tracks issues.

A payroll system processes compensation.

These systems can still fail, but the logic is usually easier to locate. The workflow is usually easier to map. The owner is usually easier to identify.

By default, AI changes that.

AI does not simply add another tool to the stack.

AI can change the game, the pieces, the players, and the rules at the same time without guidance.

That is why treating AI implementation like a normal software rollout is a dangerous business decision.

Most companies may think it is adding efficiency.

In reality, it is likely adding a layer of confident ambiguity on top of processes that were already poorly documented.

The Current State Problem

Before an organization adds AI to a workflow, it needs to understand the workflow that already exists.

That sounds obvious.

In practice, many companies are likely skipping it if they’re desiring to be competitive in their space.

They do not fully document the current state.

They do not know where the unofficial shortcuts live.

They do not know which spreadsheet is actually running the process.

They do not know which employee has been quietly holding the workflow together through their own memory, habits, and tacit workaround logic. (doubtful they professionally care for this employee either)

They do not know which vendor owns which dependency.

They do not know what can break downstream if one step changes.

Then AI gets layered on top.

Now the organization has a new problem.

If something goes wrong, what exactly does it roll back to?

The old process was never documented clearly.

The new process may not use the same language the company does.

The AI output may look polished, but the chain underneath it is unclear.

That is not intelligence. That is ambiguity wearing a suit.

AI Can Mask Old Complexity

One of the biggest mistakes organizations make is assuming AI will clean up the mess.

It usually does not. AI often inherits the mess.

AI does not magically erase years cutting corners, skipping documentation, giving people broad access for convenience, or relying on tacit knowledge.

It just moves that history faster.

Bad data moves faster.

Weak assumptions move faster.

Unverified claims move faster.

Poorly owned workflows move faster.

The organization may feel more modern while becoming less able to explain itself.

That is the part people underestimate.

Speed without traceability is exposure.

The “Prime Suspect” Problem

There is another risk that does not get discussed enough. Organizations often give employees more access than they actually need.

Not because it is right, but easier.

Someone joins a team and gets broad permissions across tools, files, dashboards, workflows, and admin panels because the business wants the work done quickly.

Day 1 ready. All systems going, and good to go.

The problem is that broad access creates broad liability.

If something goes wrong, the person with the access becomes the person everyone wants to question.

Even if they did not design the system.

Even if they did not approve the workflow.

Even if they did not control the upstream data.

Even if the decision was above their pay grade.

That person becomes the prime suspect because the access trail points in their direction.

AI makes that risk worse.

Introducing AI tools with unclear permissions, unclear approvals, and unclear ownership, results in the organization not knowing who is actually accountable for the output.

Was it the employee?

The model?

The vendor?

The manager?

The data owner?

The team that approved the prompt?

The person who failed to review it?

The person who had access but no authority?

That ambiguity matters.

Access without clear responsibility is not empowerment, but exposure.

The Ratification Gap

A major issue with AI-generated work is that organizations may accept outputs without proper ratification.

Ratification means something is reviewed, validated, and confirmed by someone or something outside of the original claim.

That matters because AI can produce information that sounds authoritative while being wrong.

Try this: Ask an LLM the question, “what’s a brick?”, and observe it’s output.

The LLM likely described your typical mortar building unit. However, in the world, the term ‘brick’, can point to many different things, for example, colloquially, a cellular device’s status could be described as ‘brick’.

In this scenario, the LLM will have made an assumption that it did NOT make you privy of.

That is the foundation for circular logic.

The system cannot be the only witness for its own accuracy.

If AI drafts a claim about a product, policy, medication, financial result, legal requirement, customer segment, or operational process, that claim needs independent validation.

Who verified it?

What source confirmed it?

Was the source current?

Was the claim approved?

Was it checked against policy?

Was it checked against law?

Was it checked against actual business records?

If the answer is unclear, the company is not operating from intelligence, but ambiguity.

AI Incidents Need Communication Plans

Another issue is that many organizations do not have strong communication strategies for AI-related incidents.

If an AI system generates incorrect content, exposes data, misclassifies a customer, produces a false claim, or influences a bad decision, what happens next?

Who gets notified?

Who investigates?

Who owns the correction?

Who communicates with the client?

Who preserves the evidence?

Who decides whether the incident is material?

Who determines whether regulators, partners, or customers need to know?

For many organizations, those answers are not clear.

That is a problem.

Because AI does not only create technical incidents.

It creates business incidents.

Reputational incidents.

Legal incidents.

Customer trust incidents.

Operational incidents.

A company cannot wait until the mistake is public to decide who owns the response.

AI Requires a Different Implementation Mindset

AI implementation is not just another technology change.

A normal software implementation may change a workflow.

AI can change the workflow, the decision logic, the evidence trail, the speed of execution, the role of employees, and the definition of accountability all at once.

That is why organizations need to slow down before they speed up.

They need to document the current state.

They need to define ownership.

They need to limit access.

They need to validate outputs.

They need to separate test environments from production workflows.

They need to preserve audit trails.

They need to establish incident communication plans.

They need to make sure employees are not handed broad access without clear authority.

They need to know where AI is assisting, where it is deciding, and where it should not be involved at all.

The question is not simply:

“How do we use AI?”

The better question is:

“What are we allowing AI to touch, change, suggest, approve, or accelerate?”

That is where the risk lives.

The Real Lesson

AI is powerful.

But power without clarity creates risk.

If an organization cannot explain the workflow before AI, it will struggle to explain the outcome after AI.

If it cannot identify who owns the data, it will struggle to defend the decision.

If it cannot verify the claim, it should not publish the claim.

If it cannot trace who changed the record, it should not pretend the system is governed.

If it cannot roll back, it should be careful about rolling forward.

That is why I keep coming back to the phrase ambiguous intelligence.

Because the danger is not only that AI might be wrong.

The danger is that AI might be wrong in a way that sounds right, moves fast, touches real business processes, and leaves the organization unable to explain how it happened.

That is not a small issue.

That is business risk.

Before companies chase artificial intelligence, they need to reduce ambiguous intelligence.

Because confidence is not governance.

Automation is not accountability.

And intelligence without traceability is just another blind spot moving at scale.
